items.lessonTitle: under the water and back up

neighbors.heading: a prayer in the river
neighbors.text: Today the water closed over someone, and they came up new. Hindus know the river too. Pilgrims wade into the Ganga at dawn and dip under, again and again. Many say a short bathing verse that calls the holy rivers, Ganga, Yamuna, Godavari, Sarasvati, into the water in front of them. Coming up, many hear it as being washed clean.
neighbors.difference: Baptism happens once, Christians say, joining a person to Christ and his church. A Hindu river bath can be repeated at every festival and pilgrimage, and the water itself, above all the Ganga, is honored as holy, by many as a goddess.
neighbors.shared: water can mean starting clean.
neighbors.sources: Hindu bathing verse, "Gange cha Yamune chaiva" (paraphrase) · bathing in the Ganga (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: washed before you stand
neighbors.text: Today the water marked a fresh start. Muslims wash before they pray. The Qur'an says: "O ye who believe! When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows, and lightly rub your heads and (wash) your feet up to the ankles." It's called wudu: water first, then prayer.
neighbors.difference: Baptism is given once and, Christians say, joins a person to Christ. Wudu is repeated whenever it's needed before prayer, and it isn't how someone becomes Muslim; a person enters Islam by saying the shahada, the witness to one God.
neighbors.shared: you can come to God with clean hands and a fresh start.

neighbors.heading: free and undeserved
neighbors.text: Today grace was a gift nobody earns. Catholics say it plainly too. The Catechism calls grace favor: the free and undeserved help God gives, so we can answer his call and share his life. And Catholics greet the one they call full of it: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee."
neighbors.difference: Christians agree grace can't be earned. Catholics teach it comes especially through the sacraments, and that our freedom answers it and works with it. Many Protestants put the weight on grace received by faith alone.
neighbors.shared: you are loved before you've done a thing.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1996, 2001-2002 (paraphrase) · Luke 1:28 (Douay-Rheims)

neighbors.heading: by the Guru's grace
neighbors.text: Today you met grace: a gift, not a wage. Sikhs name it on the very first page of their scripture. The Mool Mantar, the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib, ends with two words: gur prasad, by the Guru's grace. And Guru Nanak's Japji says, in plain words, that deeds bring us this body, but the gate of freedom opens by God's glance of grace.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, grace comes through Jesus, whose death and rising they believe opened the way. Sikhs speak of God's nadar, a glance of grace, reaching people through the Guru's word and the Name, without a sacrifice for sin.
neighbors.shared: the best gifts arrive before we've earned them.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Mool Mantar (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib, pauri 4 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: agape: the word for love that isn't a feeling

neighbors.heading: love your neighbor, first said
neighbors.text: Today love was something you do. When Jesus named the second great commandment, he quoted the Torah: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." Jews have kept that verse close. Asked to teach the whole Torah while standing on one foot, Hillel said: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. The rest is commentary. Go and learn.
neighbors.difference: Christians read love through Jesus giving his life, and Paul's word agape. Jews learn love from the Torah's commandments, worked out in deeds like visiting the sick and comforting mourners, and not through Jesus.
neighbors.shared: love shows up as something your hands do.

neighbors.heading: a heart with no edges
neighbors.text: Today agape was love you choose, even when you don't feel it. Buddhists train a love like that: metta, loving-kindness. A short teaching of the Buddha's says to hold all beings the way a mother would protect her only child with her own life, and to let a boundless heart reach above, below and all around. Practice often starts with yourself, then widens out.
neighbors.difference: Christians say we love because God loved us first. Buddhists cultivate metta without a creator God, as a training of the heart that frees the one who practices it and blesses everyone it reaches.
neighbors.shared: love can be practiced, a little more each day.
neighbors.sources: Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (paraphrase) · 1 John 4:19

items.lessonTitle: The mustard seed and the yeast (Matthew 13:31–33)

neighbors.heading: an atom's weight
neighbors.text: Today the kingdom started as a seed you can barely see. The Qur'an counts small things too: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then." Nothing is too small to matter. Muslims also remember the Prophet teaching that the deeds God loves most are the steady ones, even if small.
neighbors.difference: Jesus's seed is the kingdom of heaven, growing by God's hand. The Qur'an's atom is about each person's own deeds, seen and weighed on the Day of Judgment.
neighbors.shared: small and faithful counts more than we think.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 99:7-8 (Pickthall 1930) · hadith on small, steady deeds, Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the tiniest sprout
neighbors.text: Today a mustard seed became a tree. Philosophers noticed the same shape in things. The Tao Te Ching says a tree too big to hug grew from a tiny sprout, a tower of nine stories rose from a small heap of earth, and a journey of a thousand miles began with a single step. Big things start small, and they start where you are.
neighbors.difference: Jesus tells of God's kingdom, growing by God's hand. The Tao Te Ching describes the natural way things unfold, the Tao, which it doesn't present as a personal God who listens or plans.
neighbors.shared: the first small step is already part of the whole way.

neighbors.heading: one row on the floor
neighbors.text: Today the host said: go out and bring them in, there's room. Gurdwaras keep a table like that: the langar, a free kitchen open to anyone. Guests sit side by side on the floor in rows, the pangat, so nobody sits higher than anyone else. The Guru Granth Sahib gives the reason in plain words: there is one Father, and we are all his children.
neighbors.difference: Jesus's banquet is a picture of God's kingdom and its open invitation. Langar is a real meal, served daily in many gurdwaras, where sitting on the same floor answers caste and rank, cooked and served by volunteers as seva.
neighbors.shared: there's always room for one more at the table.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 611, Guru Arjan (paraphrase) · langar and pangat in Sikh practice (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the guest is God
neighbors.text: Today the invitations went out to the streets and lanes. Hindus have an old saying for whoever is at the door: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you. It comes from the Taittiriya Upanishad, in the parting advice a teacher gives a student going home: honor your mother, your father, your teacher, your guest.
neighbors.difference: In the parable, God is the host and we are the guests. Atithi devo bhava turns it around: the guest is honored as divine. Christians don't call a guest God, though they say Christ is met in the stranger.
neighbors.shared: the knock at the door might be the best part of the day.

neighbors.heading: whoever would tend me
neighbors.text: Today the king said: what you did for the least, you did for me. A story in the Buddhist monks' rules sounds close. The Buddha found a monk lying sick and uncared for. He and Ananda washed him and laid him on a bed. Then he told the monks: you have no mother or father to tend you here; whoever would tend me should tend the sick.
neighbors.difference: In the parable, Christ himself is met in the hungry and the sick. The Buddha wasn't saying he lived in the sick monk; he was teaching that caring for the sick is as worthy as caring for him.
neighbors.shared: caring for someone sick is never a small thing.

neighbors.heading: half a cloak
neighbors.text: Today he wore ordinary faces. Catholics tell a story about that. Martin, a young soldier, met a freezing beggar at the gate of Amiens, cut his own cloak in two, and gave him half. That night, his biographer says, Martin dreamed of Christ wearing the half-cloak and saying Martin had clothed him. The Church calls such deeds works of mercy.
neighbors.difference: Christians share this parable. Catholics also name its deeds the corporal works of mercy and honor saints like Martin, asking their prayers. Many Protestants honor such examples too, but pray to God alone.
neighbors.shared: a coat given to a stranger is never small.
neighbors.sources: Sulpicius Severus, Life of Saint Martin, ch. 3 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase) · Matthew 25:36

neighbors.heading: what mean ye by this?
neighbors.text: Today a boy sat with the teachers, listening and asking. Jewish learning runs on questions, and the Torah expects them: "And it shall come to pass, when your children shall say unto you: What mean ye by this service?" At the Passover table, a child often asks the questions out loud. And the sages warned: a bashful person can't learn.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear Jesus's answer, "I must be about my Father's business," as an early sign of who he is. For Jews, questions belong to every child at the table, learning Torah together, with no single questioner at the center.
neighbors.shared: a child's question can be holy.
neighbors.sources: Exodus 12:26 (JPS 1917) · Pirkei Avot 2:5 (paraphrase) · the Passover seder's questions (paraphrase) · Luke 2:49 (KJV)

neighbors.heading: the examined life
neighbors.text: Today a twelve-year-old asked questions of the wisest people in the room. Philosophy started in the same place. Socrates spent his days in the marketplace of Athens, asking people what they meant by goodness and courage, and admitting what he didn't know. On trial for it, he told the jury: "the unexamined life is not worth living."
neighbors.difference: Jesus asks and listens in his Father's house, inside a tradition with scripture at its heart. Socrates asked in the open market, testing each answer by argument and reason.
neighbors.shared: a good question is a kind of respect.

neighbors.heading: a hill for an umbrella
neighbors.text: Today a storm hit and everyone in the boat panicked. Hindus tell a storm story too. When rain lashed the village of Vrindavan for days, the young Krishna lifted Govardhan hill on one finger and held it up like an umbrella. The cowherds, their families and their cows all crowded underneath, safe and dry, until the sky cleared.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus honor Krishna as God himself in human form, one of the times, age after age, that God comes to protect the good. Christians say God became human once, in Jesus, and his calming the sea shows who he is.
neighbors.shared: nobody has to ride out the storm alone.

neighbors.heading: where hearts find rest
neighbors.text: Today the friends shouted into the wind, and the sea went still. The Qur'an knows that boat. It describes people at sea when a storm wind comes and waves rise on every side: then they cry to God alone, with all their hearts. And it names where calm is found: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!"
neighbors.difference: Christians see Jesus commanding the wind as God's own power in him. Muslims honor Jesus, Isa, as a great prophet whose miracles came by God's permission; only God rules the wind and the sea.
neighbors.shared: a frightened prayer is still a prayer.

items.lessonTitle: Who do you say I am? (Matthew 16:13–20)

neighbors.heading: the keys
neighbors.text: Today Peter answered the question, and Jesus answered back. Catholics hear the next lines as the heart of their church: "thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church... And I will give to thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven." The Church teaches that the pope, the bishop of Rome, holds Peter's place as his successor.
neighbors.difference: Christians share the verse and read it differently. Catholics see Peter's office passed to the popes. Orthodox Christians honor Rome's bishop but not as head over all, and many Protestants read the rock as Peter's confession of faith.
neighbors.shared: the faith reaches us through hands that held it before.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 16:18-19 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 881-882 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the same light, a new lamp
neighbors.text: Today Peter was given a new name and a charge. Sikhs remember a handing-on too. Guru Nanak chose his devoted follower Lehna, renamed him Angad, and bowed to him as the next Guru. A hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib says it was the same light and the same way; only the body changed. The light passed on through ten Gurus.
neighbors.difference: Catholics see Peter's keys handed from person to person, pope after pope. Sikhs believe the tenth Guru ended the line of human Gurus and named the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, as the Guru from then on.
neighbors.shared: a light can pass from hand to hand and stay the same.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 966-967, the Var of Satta and Balwand (paraphrase) · Matthew 16:18

neighbors.heading: as if you came out of Egypt
neighbors.text: Today Jesus sat at a Passover table and said: remember. That table is Jewish first, and the seder still says it. The Torah tells parents: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day, saying: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." The Mishnah adds: in every generation, see yourself as if you came out.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, Passover remembers God bringing Israel out of Egypt, whole and complete in itself. At the last supper, Christians hear Jesus giving the bread and the cup a new meaning centered on himself.
neighbors.shared: remembering together turns an old story into our story.

neighbors.heading: a last meal, and a kind word
neighbors.text: Today a teacher's last meal became a way to remember him. The Buddha had a last meal too, at the home of Cunda, a metalworker. Afterward, knowing Cunda might blame himself, the Buddha sent word that this meal was a great blessing. He also named four places where followers could go to remember him: where he was born, awoke, first taught, and passed away.
neighbors.difference: Christians remember Jesus as risen and, many believe, present in the bread and cup. Buddhists remember the Buddha as a teacher who has passed fully beyond, and honor him most by practicing what he taught.
neighbors.shared: remembering someone well can change how you live.

items.lessonTitle: The beggar at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3:1–10)

neighbors.heading: a smile is charity
neighbors.text: Today Peter had no coin, and gave what he had. Muslims know that kind of giving. The Prophet Muhammad taught that every good deed is charity, and that even meeting someone with a cheerful face is a good deed not to be looked down on. The Qur'an puts kindness above a cold gift: "A kind word with forgiveness is better than almsgiving followed by injury."
neighbors.difference: Peter heals the man in the name of Jesus. In Islam, healing comes from God alone, and charity, sadaqah, is something anyone can give any day, rich or poor, alongside zakat, the set yearly giving.
neighbors.shared: you always have something to give, even with empty pockets.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:263 (Pickthall 1930) · hadith on every good deed as charity, Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (paraphrase) · hadith on a cheerful face, Sahih Muslim (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: attention is generosity
neighbors.text: Today, before anything else, Peter looked at the man and said: look on us. The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. The psychologist Carl Rogers built his work on a close idea: people grow when someone truly listens. Sometimes the gift isn't money. It's stopping, looking up, and meeting someone's eyes.
neighbors.difference: Peter gives healing in Jesus's name. Weil and Rogers describe a gift any person can give, with or without faith: full, unhurried attention that lets someone feel real.
neighbors.shared: being truly seen can change someone's whole day.
neighbors.sources: Simone Weil, letter to Joë Bousquet, 1942 (paraphrase) · Carl Rogers, On Becoming a Person (paraphrase) · Acts 3:4

neighbors.heading: your will is sweet
neighbors.text: Today two men sang in a dark prison, hurt and in chains. Sikhs remember a Guru who met suffering with the same calm. Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, was put to death for his faith. Sikh tradition links his last days to words from his own hymn: your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak asks only for the treasure of your Name.
neighbors.difference: Paul and Silas praise God through Jesus, and an earthquake opens the doors. Guru Arjan was not set free; Sikhs remember him as a martyr who accepted God's will, hukam, in peace.
neighbors.shared: a song in the dark is a kind of courage.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Guru Arjan, Raag Asa (paraphrase) · Acts 16:25

neighbors.heading: the boy who kept singing
neighbors.text: Today Paul and Silas sang at midnight, and the other prisoners listened. Hindus tell of Prahlad, a boy who would not stop singing the name of Vishnu, even when his father, a demon king, tried every cruelty to stop him. The story says he was kept safe through it all, still singing, until Vishnu came as Narasimha to protect him.
neighbors.difference: Prahlad is saved when Vishnu appears as Narasimha, half lion, half man, one of the forms many Hindus say God takes to protect the devoted. Christians pray to one God through Jesus; in Acts, an earthquake opens the doors.
neighbors.shared: a song can keep you company where nothing else can.

neighbors.heading: the noble ones
neighbors.text: Today a saint turned out to be an ordinary person made holy. Buddhists take refuge in three things: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, the community. Its noble ones came from everywhere. Upali was a barber before he became a monk and a master of the rules. Ambapali, a courtesan, became a nun, and her verses are still read.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, holiness is God's gift, worked in a person by grace. For Buddhists, the noble ones become so by practice and insight on the path the Buddha taught, without a creator God.
neighbors.shared: nobody is too ordinary for the path.
neighbors.sources: the three refuges, Khuddakapatha 1 (paraphrase) · Vinaya, Cullavagga 7.1 (paraphrase) · Therigatha, Ambapali's verses (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the communion of saints
neighbors.text: Today saint turned out to be a name for every believer. Catholics keep that, and add something. In the Creed they say: "I believe in... the communion of saints." The Church teaches that everyone is called to holiness, and it names some saints, after careful study, as models and as friends who pray for us. Their feast days fill the calendar.
neighbors.difference: Catholics and Orthodox ask saints in heaven to pray for them. Many Protestants honor the saints as examples but pray to God alone, and use saint mostly in Paul's sense: every believer.
neighbors.shared: the people who went before can still cheer us on.
neighbors.sources: Apostles' Creed · Catechism of the Catholic Church 828, 956 (paraphrase) · Lumen Gentium 40 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the divided self
neighbors.text: Today Augustine wept in a garden, pulled two ways at once. William James, the psychologist, studied that state and called it the divided self: a person at war inside, wanting two lives. He wrote about Augustine by name. James saw the split come together in many ways, sudden or slow, religious or not, and the peace afterward as a self made whole.
neighbors.difference: Augustine says his restless heart found rest in God, through Christ. James, writing as a psychologist, describes the coming together without deciding what causes it; he leaves room for God and for other answers.
neighbors.shared: a divided heart can come together again.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), lecture 8, "The Divided Self" (paraphrase) · Augustine, Confessions 8.12 · Augustine, Confessions 1.1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: as the hart panteth
neighbors.text: Today a restless heart found its rest. The Psalms knew that thirst first: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, So panteth my soul after Thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God." The same psalm asks, more than once, why are you cast down, my soul? Then answers itself: hope in God.
neighbors.difference: Augustine's longing ends in turning to Christ. For Jews, this is Israel's own psalm: the longing is for the one God of Israel, met in prayer, Torah and the gathered people, not through Jesus.
neighbors.shared: longing for God is already a prayer.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 42:2-3 (JPS 1917; Psalm 42:1-2 in many Bibles) · Psalm 42:6, 12 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the offering of a name
neighbors.text: Today one short line, said with the breath, became a whole prayer. Hindus know this as japa: a name of God or a mantra, said again and again, often on a string of beads, a mala. Ram. Om namah Shivaya. Hare Krishna. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that among offerings, he is japa, the quiet repeating.
neighbors.difference: The Jesus Prayer calls on Jesus by name and asks his mercy. Japa honors many names and forms of God, and many Hindus say God is present in the Name itself, so saying it is already being near.
neighbors.shared: a few words, said with love, can become a whole prayer.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 10.25 (paraphrase) · japa with a mala (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: remember, often
neighbors.text: Today a short prayer rode the breath, over and over. Muslims call it dhikr, remembrance. The Qur'an says: "O ye who believe! Remember Allah with much remembrance." Many Muslims repeat short phrases, often on prayer beads: glory be to God, praise be to God, God is greatest, and astaghfirullah, I ask God's forgiveness, close to have mercy on me.
neighbors.difference: The Jesus Prayer calls Jesus Lord and Son of God. Muslims honor Jesus as a prophet and call on God alone; dhikr praises God and his names, and blessings asked for the Prophet are still prayers to God.
neighbors.shared: remembering God can fit inside a single breath.

neighbors.heading: the hours of the day
neighbors.text: Today a short prayer closed the day. Catholics pray the hours too, in the Liturgy of the Hours: psalms at morning, evening and night, with Compline before sleep. A psalm behind it says: "Seven times a day I have given praise to thee." The Church calls it the prayer of the whole Church, making every hour of the day holy.
neighbors.difference: The lesson's collect comes from the Anglican prayer book. Catholics pray their own form; priests and religious promise to pray it daily, and laypeople are warmly invited. Both grew from the old monastic hours.
neighbors.shared: a little prayer at the same hour can hold a whole day.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 118:164 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 119:164 in many Bibles) · Sacrosanctum Concilium 84 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a song before sleep
neighbors.text: Today you prayed: lighten our darkness. Sikhs keep a daily rhythm of prayer too, called nitnem. Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib at dawn. Rehras Sahib in the evening. And Kirtan Sohila at night before sleep, words of praise to carry into the dark, read from a small prayer book, a gutka, or said from memory.
neighbors.difference: Christian daily prayer is built from the psalms and asks through Christ. Sikh nitnem is the Gurus' own hymns, sung or read, praising the one Creator, with the Guru's word at the center.
neighbors.shared: ending the day with a prayer makes the dark less lonely.
neighbors.sources: Sikh nitnem: Japji Sahib, Rehras Sahib, Kirtan Sohila (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: two pockets
neighbors.text: Today: dust thou art. The words are from the Torah's first pages, and Jews read them too: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." A Hasidic teacher, Rabbi Simcha Bunim, taught to carry two notes, one in each pocket. One says: I am but dust and ashes. The other: for my sake the world was created.
neighbors.difference: Ash Wednesday begins Lent and points toward the cross and Easter. The two-pockets teaching asks a person to hold both truths every day, with no season and no Christ at its center.
neighbors.shared: small and precious, both at once.
neighbors.sources: Genesis 3:19 (JPS 1917) · Genesis 18:27 · Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (paraphrase) · Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa, Hasidic tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: all created things perish
neighbors.text: Today ashes said: you won't last forever. Buddhists sit with that same truth, on purpose. The Dhammapada says: "All created things perish." Monks and laypeople practice remembering death, maranasati, not to frighten themselves but to wake up: if this breath could be the last, what matters now? Seeing it clearly, the text says, is the way to purity.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, dust is answered by God's love and the hope of resurrection. For Buddhists, seeing impermanence clearly is itself the path to freedom from suffering, with no creator God and no resurrection.
neighbors.shared: remembering we're small can make us gentle.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 277 (Max Müller 1881) · maranasati, mindfulness of death (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: give us rest with it
neighbors.text: Today a short stop still counted. Islam asks for a pause five times a day, wherever you are, to pray. When it was time, the Prophet Muhammad would say to Bilal, who gave the call: give us rest with it. And on Friday the Qur'an says: "haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading," then go back out to your work.
neighbors.difference: Jews and many Christians keep a sabbath, rooted in God resting on the seventh day. Islam has no sabbath of rest: Friday is for gathering to pray, and the Qur'an says making the heavens and earth brought God no weariness.
neighbors.shared: a pause can feel like coming home.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 62:9 (Pickthall 1930) · Qur'an 62:10 (paraphrase) · Qur'an 50:38 (paraphrase) · hadith of Bilal, Sunan Abu Dawud (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a broad margin
neighbors.text: Today sabbath started small: a phone in a drawer, a walk to nowhere. Henry David Thoreau knew that kind of stop at Walden Pond. "I love a broad margin to my life," he wrote. Some summer mornings he sat in his sunny doorway from sunrise till noon, doing nothing useful, and said he grew in those hours like corn in the night.
neighbors.difference: Sabbath is a gift and a command from God, kept as holy time, often with others. Thoreau found his stopping alone in the woods, with no command and no set day, just attention to the morning.
neighbors.shared: an unhurried hour is a gift you can give yourself.

neighbors.heading: a tenth, shared
neighbors.text: Today the tithe gave the first tenth back. Sikhs keep a tenth too: dasvandh, from das, ten. The tradition asks Sikhs to give a tenth of what they earn for the gurdwara, the langar, and people in need. Guru Nanak's way is often put in three parts: work honestly, remember God, share. The Guru Granth Sahib says one who earns by work and gives some away knows the way.
neighbors.difference: In the Bible, tithes supported the priests and Levites, and some went to the poor. Sikhs keep no priestly caste; dasvandh goes to the community's kitchen, the gurdwara and anyone in need.
neighbors.shared: what we earn grows sweeter when some of it is shared.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245 (paraphrase) · dasvandh in Sikh practice (paraphrase) · Malachi 3:10

neighbors.heading: a gift that wants nothing back
neighbors.text: Today giving came first, not last. Hindus call giving dana, and the Bhagavad Gita says what makes a gift pure: it's given because giving is right, at the right place and time, to someone worthy, who can't pay it back. A gift given to get something in return, or given grudgingly, the Gita says, is lesser.
neighbors.difference: The tithe names a share, a tenth, given to God first. The Gita sets no fixed share; it weighs a gift by the spirit behind it, freely given, wanting nothing back.
neighbors.shared: the best gifts don't keep score.

neighbors.heading: reciting together
neighbors.text: Today the first Christians taught one another by singing. Buddhists have long chanted together. Monks and nuns learned the Buddha's teachings by reciting them aloud as a group, and the early gatherings that settled the teachings were called sangiti, a reciting together. Many temples still chant daily, with words like the Metta Sutta.
neighbors.difference: Christians sing praise to God, through Christ. Buddhist chanting usually recites the Buddha's teaching, to remember it, take it to heart, and steady the mind, rather than to praise a creator.
neighbors.shared: a voice joined with others carries further than one.
neighbors.sources: the early councils, sangiti, in Buddhist tradition (paraphrase) · Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: pride of place
neighbors.text: Today the church was born singing. Catholics keep a very old song alive: Gregorian chant, the psalms and prayers of the Mass sung in long, simple lines. The Second Vatican Council called sacred music part of worship itself, and gave chant pride of place in the Roman liturgy. Every Mass prays the angels' song from Isaiah: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts."
neighbors.difference: Catholics center song on the Mass, with chant honored first among styles. Many Protestant churches, from Luther on, built worship around hymns the whole congregation sings, which the next days explore.
neighbors.shared: singing together is one more way to pray.

neighbors.heading: a retreat inside
neighbors.text: Today the psalm said: drop it, stop. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself about the same need: "Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains." But, he said, you can retreat any time into your own mind, and there's no quieter place. So give yourself this retreat often, and begin again.
neighbors.difference: The psalm's stillness is about knowing God, who makes wars cease. Marcus, a Stoic, retreats into his own reason, to set his thoughts in order, more than to meet a God who speaks.
neighbors.shared: there's a quiet place inside you, open any time.

neighbors.heading: an hour before praying
neighbors.text: Today: be still, and know. That psalm is a Jewish song first.The Mishnah remembers the pious ones of old, who would wait an hour before they prayed, to turn their hearts toward God. Even if a king greeted them, it says, they wouldn't answer, and even if a snake wound round their heel, they wouldn't stop.
neighbors.difference: Christians pray Psalm 46 within the Christian Bible, often alongside Jesus's words. For Jews, it is Israel's own psalm, and stillness readies the heart for the Amidah, the standing prayer.
neighbors.shared: a quiet moment first makes room for everything after.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah Berakhot 5:1 (paraphrase) · Psalm 46:11 (Psalm 46:10 in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: what true austerity is
neighbors.text: Today Isaiah said the real fast is loosing chains and sharing bread. The Bhagavad Gita also asks what true austerity, tapas, is. Its answer reaches past the body's hunger: honoring the gods, teachers and the wise, purity, straightness, self-restraint, and not harming anyone. And there's tapas of speech too: words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah speaks for God, calling the fast into justice for the hungry and the oppressed. The Gita's tapas is a discipline of body, speech and mind, offered without wanting a reward.
neighbors.shared: going without is meant to make us kinder.

neighbors.heading: fasting that feeds
neighbors.text: Today the fast God chose was feeding the hungry. Muslims fast through Ramadan, and the Qur'an says why: "O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)." Those who can't fast may feed someone in need instead, and the month ends with a gift so the poor can celebrate too.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah's fast is set by the God of Israel, and Christian fasts vary by church and season. Ramadan is one month, dawn to sunset, asked of every adult Muslim who is able, and it ends with Eid al-Fitr.
neighbors.shared: an empty stomach can open a full heart.

items.lessonTitle: A mother-in-law and a whole town (Mark 1:29–39)

neighbors.heading: deacons, the servers
neighbors.text: Today a healed woman got up and served: diakoneo, the root of deacon. Catholics still ordain deacons. In Acts, the apostles chose seven men "of good reputation, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom" to serve the tables, and tradition calls them the first deacons. Deacons today, some of them married, proclaim the Gospel, baptize, witness weddings, and serve the poor.
neighbors.difference: Catholics, with Orthodox Christians and Anglicans, ordain deacons as clergy. In many Protestant churches, deacons are lay members chosen to serve. Every church still hears the same word in it: servant.
neighbors.shared: the one who serves the table is honored there.
neighbors.sources: Acts 6:3 (Douay-Rheims) · Acts 6:1-6 · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1569-1571 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seva
neighbors.text: Today a woman served, and the word was the one Jesus used for his own work. Sikhs call service seva, and it's everywhere in a gurdwara: cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, minding shoes at the door. Guru Nanak says it plainly: serve in the midst of this world, and you'll be given a seat of honor in God's court.
neighbors.difference: In Mark, she serves Jesus, whom Christians call Lord. Sikh seva is offered to everyone, as service to the Guru and to God present in all, done humbly, without wanting thanks.
neighbors.shared: serving others turns ordinary chores into something holy.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Guru Nanak, Sri Raag (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a hand to lift you
neighbors.text: Today four friends dug through a roof for one man. Jewish wisdom prizes friends like that: "Two are better than one... For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow." The Talmud tells of a sick rabbi raised up by a friend who took his hand, because, it says, a prisoner can't free himself from prison.
neighbors.difference: In Mark, the friends' faith brings the man to Jesus, who forgives and heals him. In the Talmud, one teacher lifts another, a healing between friends, with no Messiah in the room, only God and each other.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the most faithful thing is to carry a friend.

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today a man reached Jesus because of his friends. The Buddha said something striking about friends. His attendant Ananda once said good friendship must be half of the holy life. The Buddha answered: not so, Ananda. Good friendship is the whole of the holy life. Someone with good friends, he said, can be expected to walk the path.
neighbors.difference: The friends carry the man to Jesus, who heals him. For Buddhists, good friends hold you up, but no one can walk the path for you; the Dhammapada says you must make the effort yourself, and the Buddhas only point the way.
neighbors.shared: good friends can get you where you couldn't go alone.

neighbors.heading: who makes it grow?
neighbors.text: Today the farmer planted, slept, and the seed grew, he knew not how. The Qur'an asks the farmer a question: "Have ye seen that which ye cultivate? Is it ye who foster it, or are We the Fosterer?" You dig, you sow, you wait. The growing, the Qur'an says, belongs to God.
neighbors.difference: Jesus tells the seed as a parable of God's kingdom, growing unseen. The Qur'an points to the real field as a sign of God's power, and adds that God could turn the crop to chaff, so the farmer stays grateful.
neighbors.shared: you plant, you rest, and the growing isn't all yours.

neighbors.heading: it grows while you sleep
neighbors.text: Today the seed grew while the farmer slept. Psychologists found something like it. John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach had people learn nonsense syllables, then either sleep or stay awake. After the same hours, the sleepers remembered more. Later research suggests the sleeping brain sorts and keeps what the day planted. You do the work; rest does some too.
neighbors.difference: Mark tells the story about God's kingdom, and the growing belongs to God. The psychology describes a brain at work in the dark, and makes no claim about God either way.
neighbors.shared: some of the best growing happens once you stop pushing.
neighbors.sources: Jenkins & Dallenbach, "Obliviscence during sleep and waking" (1924) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: after the prayer, the kitchen
neighbors.text: Today the miracle ended with: give her something to eat. Sikhs build that into the gurdwara. Beside the prayer hall is the langar, a free kitchen where anyone, of any faith or none, sits on the floor side by side and is fed. The Guru Granth Sahib praises the one who works for what they eat and gives some of it away.
neighbors.difference: In Mark, the meal follows a miracle Christians read as Jesus's power over death. For Sikhs, the langar isn't a sign of power but everyday seva, a practice they trace to Guru Nanak, where no one is served above anyone else.
neighbors.shared: holy moments end at the table, with someone fed.

neighbors.heading: the guest is a god
neighbors.text: Today, after the girl got up, Jesus said: give her something to eat. Hindu homes carry a teaching about the person who needs feeding. The Taittiriya Upanishad tells the student leaving his teacher: let your mother be a god to you, your father, your teacher, and your guest. Atithi devo bhava. Feeding someone is a way of honoring the sacred.
neighbors.difference: In Mark, the food comes after Jesus raises a child, and Christians read it as a sign of his power over death. In the Upanishad, honoring the guest is a householder's daily duty, tied to no miracle.
neighbors.shared: a hungry person at your table is never an interruption.

neighbors.heading: it starts in the mind
neighbors.text: Today Jesus moved the question from the plate to the heart. The Dhammapada begins in the same place: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." And: "If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage."
neighbors.difference: For Jesus, what comes out of the heart is what defiles a person before God. The Buddha speaks of no creator: harmful thoughts bring suffering by cause and effect, and the mind can be trained clear.
neighbors.shared: what comes out of you starts long before you speak.

neighbors.heading: thought, word and deed
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said evil comes from within, out of the heart. Catholics carry that into an old prayer of confession, the Confiteor, which admits sin "in thought, word, and deed." The thought comes first. The Church teaches that sin is rooted in the heart, and invites an examination of conscience before confession.
neighbors.difference: All Christians read this teaching. Catholics also bring what the heart has done to the sacrament of confession, where a priest speaks God's forgiveness; many Protestants confess straight to God, without a priest.
neighbors.shared: the cleaning starts on the inside, where no one else can see.
neighbors.sources: Confiteor (traditional English) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1853 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: faith that makes the fact
neighbors.text: Today a father prayed: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. The psychologist William James defended starting with half. In "The Will to Believe" he argued that some things only come true if we move toward them before we're sure: "faith in a fact can help create the fact." Trusting a friendship, he said, is often what makes it real.
neighbors.difference: The father brings his half-faith to Jesus and asks him to make up the rest. James wrote as a philosopher about any belief, and didn't say who, if anyone, fills the gap.
neighbors.shared: you can start with the half you have.

neighbors.heading: how long? and still, trust
neighbors.text: Today a father cried: I believe; help my unbelief. Psalm 13 holds both in one prayer. It opens: "How long, O LORD, wilt Thou forget me for ever?" A few lines later: "But as for me, in Thy mercy do I trust." Jewish prayer has room for the question and the trust, said to God in one breath.
neighbors.difference: In Mark, the father brings his doubt to Jesus, and Christians read the healing as Jesus's answer. Jews pray the psalm directly to God, and the psalm itself ends in trust before any answer comes.
neighbors.shared: doubt and trust can share one honest prayer.

neighbors.heading: let go, then enjoy
neighbors.text: Today Jesus looked at a man, loved him, and asked him to give it all away. The Isha Upanishad opens on the same theme. It says all this world is dwelt in by the Lord; let go of it, and then enjoy, and do not covet anyone's wealth. Some Hindus take that to its end in sannyasa, leaving property behind entirely.
neighbors.difference: Jesus asks one man to sell everything and follow him. The Upanishad speaks to everyone, and the letting go is first inward; many Hindus live it as householders, holding what they have loosely rather than giving it all away.
neighbors.shared: what you hold loosely can't hold you.

neighbors.heading: spend what you love
neighbors.text: Today Jesus asked a rich man to give to the poor, and he went away grieved. The Qur'an sets a similar bar: "Ye will not attain unto piety until ye spend of that which ye love. And whatsoever ye spend, Allah is aware thereof." Giving the leftovers is easy. The test is the thing you'd rather keep.
neighbors.difference: Jesus asks this one man for everything, and to follow him. Islam sets a yearly share, zakat, for every Muslim with enough wealth, and the Prophet advised a man not to give away so much that his family would be left in need.
neighbors.shared: the gift that costs you something says the most.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 3:92 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari 2742, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his bequest (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: servant of the servants
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said he came not to be served, but to serve. Catholics act it out on Holy Thursday, when in many parishes the priest kneels and washes people's feet, as Jesus did. And an old title of the pope carries the same idea: servus servorum Dei, servant of the servants of God.
neighbors.difference: Christians share this verse. Catholics also see it lived through the ordained ministry, with the pope and bishops holding real authority that they're called to use as service; many Protestants stress the servanthood of every believer, with no pope.
neighbors.shared: the best seat is the one you give up for someone else.
neighbors.sources: Mark 10:45 · Roman Missal, Holy Thursday washing of feet (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the work of the hands
neighbors.text: Today Jesus turned the best seats upside down: the first must be servant of all. Sikhs call that seva, selfless service. In the gurdwara, anyone might be scrubbing pots, sweeping the floor, or handing out roti. The Guru Granth Sahib says that by serving in this world, a person is given a place of honor in the Lord's court.
neighbors.difference: Jesus speaks of giving his life as a ransom for many, which Christians see as his alone. In Sikhism, seva isn't one person's sacrifice for others; it's every Sikh's daily path, done humbly, to wear away the ego.
neighbors.shared: serving well never made anyone smaller.

neighbors.heading: hear, O Israel
neighbors.text: Today Jesus answered from his own people's scripture. Jews still pray it, morning and night: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." The words go on the doorpost, in the mezuzah, as Deuteronomy says.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, the Shema is the heart of God's covenant with Israel, lived through the commandments. Christians hear it through Jesus, and most confess God as Trinity, which Jews do not; both say God is one.
neighbors.shared: love God, love the person beside you: an old pair, still together.

neighbors.heading: as yourself
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said to love your neighbor as yourself. The Buddha built kindness on that same "as yourself." The Dhammapada says everyone trembles at harm and everyone loves life; see that others are like you, and do no harm. Buddhists grow it into metta, loving-kindness, wished for every being, the way a mother guards her only child.
neighbors.difference: Jesus joins love of neighbor to love of one God. The Buddha's teaching doesn't rest on a creator; kindness grows from seeing that every being, like you, wants to be happy and free of pain.
neighbors.shared: the person next to you wants what you want: to be safe.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 129–130 (paraphrase) · Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: despair not
neighbors.text: Today Peter denied his friend three times, then wept. Islam has a door for that moment: tawba, turning back. The Qur'an says: "O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."
neighbors.difference: Christians read Peter's tears in the light of Jesus, who later restores him; for them, forgiveness comes through Christ. In Islam, a person turns directly to Allah, and sincere tawba is accepted.
neighbors.shared: falling hard isn't the end; turning back is the start.

neighbors.heading: guilt, not shame
neighbors.text: Today Peter wept, and the weeping was where he started again. Psychologist June Tangney's research draws a line here. Guilt says: I did a bad thing. Shame says: I am bad. In her studies, people prone to guilt tended to apologize and repair, while people prone to shame tended to hide or lash out.
neighbors.difference: Mark tells Peter's tears inside a larger story of Jesus's forgiveness. The psychology names no forgiver; it shows only that regret aimed at what you did, not at who you are, helps people make things right.
neighbors.shared: a failure can be something you did, not who you are.

neighbors.heading: your will is sweet
neighbors.text: Today Jesus prayed a psalm from the cross, and the women stayed. Sikhs remember their own Guru in agony. Tradition says that Guru Arjan, tortured in Lahore, held to the words of his own hymn: your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak begs only for the treasure of the Name. Sikhs honor him as a martyr.
neighbors.difference: Jesus's cry asks God why. Guru Arjan's line accepts God's will as sweet. Christians see Jesus's death as saving the world; Sikhs honor the Guru's death as courage for truth, not a sacrifice for sin.
neighbors.shared: even in the worst hour, the prayer still goes to God.

neighbors.heading: a cry in the hall
neighbors.text: Today Jesus cried out: my God, why hast thou forsaken me? The Mahabharata has a cry like it. Draupadi is dragged into the gambling hall, and her husbands and most of the elders sit silent. In the telling many Hindus know, she calls on Krishna, and as they pull at her sari, it keeps on coming, without end.
neighbors.difference: In that telling, Krishna answers at once and saves Draupadi's honor. In Mark, no rescue comes: Jesus dies, and Christians read that silence as part of God's saving love, answered on the third day.
neighbors.shared: when everyone else goes silent, the cry still has somewhere to go.
neighbors.sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, the dice game (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a mustard seed for grief
neighbors.text: Today Jesus blessed those who mourn. Buddhists tell of Kisa Gotami, carrying her dead child, begging the Buddha for medicine. Bring me a mustard seed, he said, from a house where no one has died. She went door to door. Every house had lost someone. She laid her child to rest, and her grief found company.
neighbors.difference: Jesus promises comfort, someone called to your side. The Buddha's comfort is seeing clearly that loss touches every house and that all things change; it doesn't rest on a promise from God.
neighbors.shared: yours is not the only house that has known loss.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada commentary on verse 114, story of Kisa Gotami (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the mother who stayed
neighbors.text: Today Jesus blessed those who mourn. Catholics keep a picture of that grief: Mary at the cross. An old hymn, the Stabat Mater, sings: "At the cross her station keeping, stood the mournful Mother weeping, close to Jesus to the last." Catholics honor her as Our Lady of Sorrows, a mother who knows.
neighbors.difference: All Christians remember Mary at the cross; John's Gospel puts her there. Catholics also ask her to pray for them in their grief and keep a feast of her sorrows; many Protestants honor her but pray to God alone.
neighbors.shared: someone who has wept will sit beside you while you weep.
neighbors.sources: Stabat Mater, tr. Edward Caswall (1849) · John 19:25

neighbors.heading: the repair attempt
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said: leave your gift at the altar, go, make it right first. Psychologist John Gottman studied couples and found that fighting alone doesn't predict a breakup. What matters is the repair attempt: a joke, a touch, a "let's start over." Couples who make repairs, and accept them, tend to last.
neighbors.difference: Jesus ties making peace with your neighbor to worship; the neighbor comes before the altar. Gottman's research is about relationships alone, and says nothing about God or worship.
neighbors.shared: the first step back toward someone is worth more than being right.
neighbors.sources: John Gottman, The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work (1999) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: first, your neighbor
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said to leave the gift at the altar and be reconciled first. The Mishnah teaches something close about Yom Kippur: the Day of Atonement atones for wrongs between a person and God, but for wrongs against another person, it doesn't atone until you make peace with them. So before Yom Kippur, many Jews go and ask forgiveness.
neighbors.difference: Jesus tells it as a story about a gift at the altar, and Christians hear it as his teaching. In Judaism it's law, tied to the yearly Day of Atonement, and later rabbis say to ask more than once if refused.
neighbors.shared: the person you hurt comes before the prayer.

neighbors.heading: the hidden gift
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said to give so quietly your left hand doesn't know what your right is doing. Hindus have a name for that: gupt daan, a secret gift, given without your name on it. The Bhagavad Gita calls the purest, sattvic gift the one given simply because giving is right, to someone who can't repay, at the right time and place.
neighbors.difference: Jesus says the Father who sees in secret will reward. The Gita praises giving with no thought of reward at all, a duty done for its own sake, and many Hindus offer the gift to God.
neighbors.shared: the best gifts don't need a name card.

neighbors.heading: the left hand doesn't know
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said: let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth. Muslims know almost the same words. The Prophet named seven whom God shades on a day with no other shade; one gives charity so secretly that his left hand doesn't know what his right gave. The Qur'an: "If ye hide it and give it to the poor, it will be better for you."
neighbors.difference: Jesus teaches this as his own word. In Islam the saying is the Prophet Muhammad's, and the Qur'an also calls open giving good, since zakat is a public duty; secret giving is praised as better.
neighbors.shared: God sees the gift no one else did.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 1423 and Sahih Muslim 1031, the seven given shade (paraphrase) · Qur'an 2:271 (Pickthall 1930)

neighbors.heading: my little sisters the birds
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said: behold the fowls of the air. Francis of Assisi took him at his word. The Little Flowers of St. Francis tells of him preaching to a flock of birds: you sow not and reap not, he told them, and God feeds you, so praise him. The birds, the story goes, stayed still until he blessed them.
neighbors.difference: All Christians read Jesus's words about the birds. Catholics also hold up Francis, a canonized saint, as a living picture of them and honor him as patron of ecology; many Protestants admire Francis without asking saints' prayers.
neighbors.shared: look closely at a bird, and worry gets a little smaller.
neighbors.sources: The Little Flowers of St. Francis, ch. 16 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: who feeds the young ones?
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said: behold the birds, God feeds them. Sikhs pray something close every evening, in Rehras. The kunj birds fly hundreds of miles, leaving their young behind. Who feeds them? Who teaches them to feed themselves? So why, O mind, do you scheme and worry, when the Lord himself provides?
neighbors.difference: Jesus calls God Father and says you are worth more than the birds. The Guru's hymn speaks of the one Creator who cares for every creature, and invites remembering the Name, Naam, in place of worry.
neighbors.shared: the one who feeds the birds has not forgotten you.

neighbors.heading: we will do, and we will hear
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said the wise builder hears and does. At Sinai, Exodus says, the people answered: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew, na'aseh v'nishma: we will do, and we will hear. Doing comes first. Pirkei Avot says it plainly: not study but doing is the main thing.
neighbors.difference: Jesus calls his own sayings the rock to build on. For Jews, the doing is the Torah's commandments, kept as a people in covenant with God, and study itself counts as one of them.
neighbors.shared: the house stands on what you do, not just what you heard.

neighbors.heading: a flower with no scent
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said hearing isn't enough; the wise build by doing. The Dhammapada puts it in a picture: "Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly." Lovely to look at. Nothing that lasts.
neighbors.difference: Jesus points to his own words as the rock, with God as judge. The Buddha asked followers to test his teaching in practice, and freedom comes through their own effort, not a creator's verdict.
neighbors.shared: words you live outlast words you only admire.

neighbors.heading: everything is praising
neighbors.text: Today Francis praised God for brother sun and sister water. The Qur'an hears creation singing too: "The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein praise Him, and there is not a thing but hymneth His praise; but ye understand not their praise." Sun, rain, stone: each praising in its own way.
neighbors.difference: Francis calls sun and water brother and sister, family to us. The Qur'an speaks of creatures as signs, ayat, pointing to God, and of people as trustees of the earth.
neighbors.shared: the whole world was praying long before we joined in.

neighbors.heading: hitched to everything else
neighbors.text: Today Francis called the sun his brother and the earth his sister. John Muir, walking the Sierra Nevada, put it as a naturalist: "When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the Universe." For Muir, kinship with the living world was simply what close looking shows.
neighbors.difference: Francis praises God through every creature, and the kinship flows from one Maker. Muir's line rests on watching nature closely, and asks no one to share a creed.
neighbors.shared: you are kin to the water you drink.
neighbors.sources: John Muir, My First Summer in the Sierra (1911)

neighbors.heading: hands at work, heart with God
neighbors.text: Today Brother Lawrence turned his omelet for the love of God. Sikh teaching makes that a daily rule: kirat karo, work honestly, and naam japo, remember God. A line from the saint Namdev, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, says: with your hands and feet do all your work, and keep your mind with the Pure Lord.
neighbors.difference: Brother Lawrence lived as a lay brother in a monastery. Sikhism asks for the same in ordinary family life; the Gurus turned away from monastic withdrawal, so work, family and prayer belong together.
neighbors.shared: God is as near at the stove as at the altar.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Saloks of Kabir, Namdev's line (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: whatever you do, offer it
neighbors.text: Today Brother Lawrence found God among the pots. Krishna says something close in the Bhagavad Gita: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, do it as an offering to me. Hindus call this karma yoga, the way of action: ordinary work, done without clutching at the result, becomes worship.
neighbors.difference: Brother Lawrence talked with God in plain words while he worked, as with a friend. Krishna's teaching adds letting go of the fruit of action: do the work, offer it, and don't cling to how it turns out.
neighbors.shared: the dishes can be a prayer, if you let them.

neighbors.heading: come back, gently
neighbors.text: Today the mystics' secret turned out to be attention, held for years. The Buddha taught it as mindfulness, sati: noticing the breath, the body, feelings and the mind, just as they are. When the mind wanders, you notice, and come back. In the Satipatthana Sutta he calls this a direct path past sorrow.
neighbors.difference: Christian mystics pay attention to God, to someone who loves them back. Buddhist mindfulness pays attention to what is happening here and now, and its goal is clear seeing and freedom, not meeting a God.
neighbors.shared: every deep thing begins with simply noticing.

neighbors.heading: where was God today?
neighbors.text: Today the mystics turned out to be people who paid attention for years. Catholics have a nightly way in: the Examen, from Ignatius of Loyola. You look back over the day with thanks, and ask where God was in it, where you turned away, and what tomorrow needs. A few minutes, every night, that train you to notice.
neighbors.difference: Many Christians reflect on their day. The Examen comes from a Catholic saint and the Jesuit order, and Catholics often pair it with confession; other churches use it too, sometimes without the sacrament.
neighbors.shared: a day looked back on kindly is a day you really lived.

neighbors.heading: by their fruits
neighbors.text: Today John Wesley's heart was strangely warmed. Later, the psychologist William James gathered stories like that in The Varieties of Religious Experience. He took such moments seriously, as real experiences that change how people live, and judged them, borrowing Jesus's words, by their fruits: did the life grow kinder, braver, more whole?
neighbors.difference: For Wesley, the warmth was assurance from God that Christ had taken away his sins. James, as a psychologist, studied what such experiences do in a life, and left open where they come from.
neighbors.shared: a warmed heart shows in the life that follows.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: God wants the heart
neighbors.text: Today Wesley's heart was strangely warmed, and Methodists asked each other: how is it with your soul? The Talmud has a short saying: Rachmana liba ba'i, the Merciful One wants the heart. Jewish prayer has a word for that inner turn, kavanah, intention: saying the words with your heart in them.
neighbors.difference: Wesley's warmth came as trust in Christ for salvation. In Judaism the heart is given to God through prayer and the commandments themselves, done with kavanah.
neighbors.shared: the words matter more when your heart is in them.

neighbors.heading: born of joy
neighbors.text: Today Genesis said God saw everything he had made, and it was very good. The Taittiriya Upanishad tells of a seeker, Bhrigu, who searched for where the world comes from, and found at last: from bliss, ananda, beings are born; by bliss they live; into bliss they go at the end.
neighbors.difference: In Genesis, God makes a world distinct from himself; Christians teach he made it from nothing. In the Upanishad, beings come from Brahman, bliss itself, and return to it; the world isn't set apart from its source in the same way.
neighbors.shared: the world began in goodness, not by accident.

neighbors.heading: everything made good
neighbors.text: Today Genesis said creation was very good. The Qur'an speaks of God "Who made all things good which He created, and He began the creation of man from clay." It also tells of the heavens and the earth made in six days, as Genesis does.
neighbors.difference: Genesis says God rested on the seventh day. The Qur'an says no weariness touched God in creating, and Muslims keep no sabbath of rest; Friday is their day of gathered prayer.
neighbors.shared: you were made on purpose, and the making was good.

neighbors.heading: a friend who prays for you
neighbors.text: Today the creed spoke of the communion of saints. Catholics live it in prayer: they ask Mary and the saints to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend. On All Saints' Day the Church remembers them all, and the next day, All Souls', it prays for those who have died.
neighbors.difference: All Christians say this line of the creed. Catholics ask the saints' prayers and pray for the souls in purgatory; many Protestants honor the saints as examples and pray to God alone.
neighbors.shared: death doesn't end the family.

neighbors.heading: remembered in every prayer
neighbors.text: Today the creed said the living and the dead are one family. Sikhs feel that whenever they pray Ardas, the standing prayer. It remembers the Gurus by name, then the Sikhs who gave their lives, who served, who kept faith, and asks the gathering to call them to mind. The sangat, the holy company, holds past and present together.
neighbors.difference: Catholics ask the saints to pray for them. Sikhs don't pray to the Gurus' companions or the martyrs; they remember them, and the prayer itself is offered to Waheguru, the one God.
neighbors.shared: the people who kept faith before you are remembered when you pray.

neighbors.heading: we have sinned
neighbors.text: Today Paul quoted the Psalms: there is none righteous, no, not one. The Hebrew Bible says it too: "For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not." On Yom Kippur, Jews confess together, in the plural: we have sinned, we have betrayed. Not I alone. We.
neighbors.difference: Paul builds from this toward grace through Christ, and many Christians speak of original sin. Judaism doesn't teach original sin; each person has a good and a bad inclination, and can always turn back, teshuvah.
neighbors.shared: nobody gets to stand on the balcony and look down.

neighbors.heading: the three roots
neighbors.text: Today Paul said none is righteous, no, not one. The Buddha named three roots of what goes wrong in us: greed, hatred and delusion. They grow in every untrained mind, not just in the people we'd like to blame. The Dhammapada adds a familiar warning: the faults of others are easy to see; our own are hard to see.
neighbors.difference: Paul speaks of sin against God, healed by God's grace. The Buddha speaks of unwholesome roots, not sin against a creator; they are pulled up through understanding and practice.
neighbors.shared: the finger that points out can point back at us too.

neighbors.heading: with hardship, ease
neighbors.text: Today Paul said trouble grows patience, character and hope. The Qur'an calls that patience sabr: "Give glad tidings to the steadfast, Who say, when a misfortune striketh them: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." And it promises, twice in a row: "Lo! with hardship goeth ease."
neighbors.difference: Paul grounds hope in God's love, shown in Christ dying for sinners. The Qur'an grounds it in trust that everything returns to Allah, who tests people and rewards the patient.
neighbors.shared: hard days can grow something easy ones can't.

neighbors.heading: growth after the storm
neighbors.text: Today Paul traced a chain: trouble, endurance, tested character, hope. Psychologists Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun named what many people report after a hard season: post-traumatic growth. Not that suffering is good, but that some come out with closer friendships, new strength, and a clearer sense of what matters.
neighbors.difference: Paul says hope doesn't disappoint because God's love has been poured into the heart. The psychology describes growth some people find, not all, and makes no promise about why.
neighbors.shared: pain doesn't get to be the whole story of a hard season.

neighbors.heading: answer evil with good
neighbors.text: Today Paul said: overcome evil with good. Sheikh Farid, whose verses are kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, says it close: Farid, answer evil with goodness; don't fill your mind with anger. Then, he says, your body won't fall sick, and you'll gain everything.
neighbors.difference: Paul quotes Proverbs and leaves vengeance to God, in the light of Christ's love for enemies. For Sikhs, Farid's line is Gurbani, and Sikh teaching also honors defending the weak, so goodness never means letting injustice go.
neighbors.shared: kindness to someone who wronged you can change two people.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Ang 1381–1382 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: win anger with calm
neighbors.text: Today Paul said to overcome evil with good. In the Mahabharata, the wise counselor Vidura gives a teaching still widely quoted: conquer anger with calm, the wicked with goodness, the miser with giving, and the liar with truth.
neighbors.difference: Paul ties it to God's judgment and Christ's love for enemies. Vidura gives it as counsel about dharma, right living, and the Mahabharata also honors those who must fight for justice.
neighbors.shared: the answer to harm doesn't have to look like harm.

neighbors.heading: the sisters' songs
neighbors.text: Today Paul greeted Phoebe and named the women of the church one by one. Buddhists keep an old book of women's voices: the Therigatha, verses of the elder nuns. Each poem comes under a name, Patacara, Kisa Gotami, Mutta, and many tell how she found freedom, often after grief.
neighbors.difference: Paul's women serve a church gathered around Christ. The nuns of the Therigatha speak of awakening through their own practice, freedom from craving, with no creator in view.
neighbors.shared: every name on the list was a whole life.

neighbors.heading: names said at the altar
neighbors.text: Today Paul ended his letter with names, many of them women. Catholics still say names at the altar. The Roman Canon, an ancient prayer of the Mass, remembers saints by name, among them Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia and Anastasia. And Phoebe herself is listed among the Church's saints.
neighbors.difference: All Christians read Romans 16. Catholics also name saints in the Mass and ask their prayers; many Protestant churches remember them as examples, without asking their prayers.
neighbors.shared: being remembered by name is a kind of love.
neighbors.sources: Roman Missal, Eucharistic Prayer I (the Roman Canon) · Roman Martyrology, 3 September (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no one would choose it
neighbors.text: Today God looked at the man by himself and said, not good. A philosopher reached the same place by watching people. Aristotle wrote that we are social by nature, and about friends he was blunt: "without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods." A full house and a full purse, with no one to share them, isn't a good life.
neighbors.difference: In Genesis, God sees the loneliness and makes a partner who fits. Aristotle needs no garden and no God here: he reasons from human nature that we're made to live among others, and that we grow good friendships ourselves.
neighbors.shared: nobody is meant to carry a life alone.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (W. D. Ross translation, 1908); Politics I.2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a friend, or death
neighbors.text: Today's "not good" is a Jewish verse too, and the rabbis kept its lesson alive. The Talmud tells of Honi, who slept for seventy years. He woke, and no one in the study hall knew him or believed who he was. Heartbroken, he prayed to die. The rabbis drew one saying from it: either companionship or death.
neighbors.difference: Christians often hear the garden story through Jesus, who quoted it about marriage. Jewish teachers carried it into learning as well: Torah is often studied in pairs, with a chavruta, a partner who argues with you and keeps you company.
neighbors.shared: we all need someone who knows our name.

neighbors.heading: a fish's warning
neighbors.text: Today the waters rose and God shut Noah in. An old Hindu text tells of a flood too. Manu, an ancestor of humankind, saves a tiny fish, and the fish warns him: a flood is coming, build a ship. When the waters rise, Manu ties his ship to the fish's horn and is pulled to a northern mountain. Later Hindu stories say the fish was Vishnu himself.
neighbors.difference: Genesis gives a reason: the earth was full of violence, and God saves Noah's family and the animals. The Brahmana gives no reason, and Manu survives alone; a new humanity begins from him and his offering.
neighbors.shared: in the deepest water, someone is still looking out for you.

neighbors.heading: in god's name, sail
neighbors.text: Today the fountains of the deep broke open. Muslims tell the flood too, with Noah, Nuh, as a prophet who warned his people for years. When the ark is ready, the Qur'an gives his words: "Embark therein! In the name of Allah be its course and its mooring." Muslims say bismillah, in the name of God, at the start of things.
neighbors.difference: In Genesis, Noah's whole family boards. In the Qur'an, one of Nuh's sons refuses, saying he'll climb a mountain, and is lost in the waves while his father calls to him: grief inside the rescue.
neighbors.shared: begin the hard journey with god's name on your lips.

neighbors.heading: every guest as christ
neighbors.text: Today Abraham ran to feed three strangers. Catholic monks turned that run into a rule. Saint Benedict told his monks to welcome every guest as Christ himself, because Christ will say, I was a stranger and you took me in. The abbot was to pour water on the guests' hands, and the whole community was to wash their feet.
neighbors.difference: Every Christian can read Mamre as a call to welcome. Catholic religious life built it into the daily rule of the monastery, so a guest house and a greeting at the door became part of how monks pray.
neighbors.shared: the stranger at your door deserves your best bread.
neighbors.sources: Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 53 (paraphrase); Matthew 25:35

neighbors.heading: the true bargain
neighbors.text: Today a morsel of bread became a feast for strangers. Sikhs tell a story of young Guru Nanak. His father gave him money to make a good deal at the market. On the way he met hungry holy men and spent it all feeding them. That, he said, was the true bargain. Gurdwaras keep a langar, a free kitchen open to anyone.
neighbors.difference: Abraham's guests turn out to be messengers bringing God's promise. In langar, no one asks who you are: everyone sits side by side on the floor and eats the same food, whatever their caste or creed.
neighbors.shared: whoever comes hungry, there's a place for them.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition, the sacha sauda story (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the place
neighbors.text: Today Jacob woke and said: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." Jewish teachers noticed the word place. The rabbis call God HaMakom, the Place, because he is the place of the world, and the world is not his place. Jews still use that name when they comfort mourners.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear Jesus pick up Jacob's ladder: he told Nathanael he'd see angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man. Jewish readers have their own readings; one finds God present wherever a person wakes.
neighbors.shared: the ordinary ground under you can be holy.

neighbors.heading: a jewel in your coat
neighbors.text: Today Jacob found God had been there all along, and he hadn't known. The Lotus Sutra tells of a poor man whose friend sewed a priceless jewel into his coat while he slept. He wandered for years, scraping by, never knowing. When they met again, the friend showed him: you were rich the whole time.
neighbors.difference: Jacob discovers God present in a place. In the Lotus Sutra, the jewel stands for the awakening the Buddha planted in his followers long before; Buddhists don't speak of a creator God here.
neighbors.shared: what you're looking for may already be right here.
neighbors.sources: Lotus Sutra, chapter 8, the parable of the jewel in the robe (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a word in the pit
neighbors.text: Today Joseph was thrown into a dry pit. Muslims know this story well: Yusuf has a whole surah of the Qur'an. And there, in the pit, Allah speaks to him: "Thou wilt tell them of this deed of theirs when they know (thee) not." His father Yaqub meets the bloodied shirt with "comely patience."
neighbors.difference: Genesis is silent while Joseph is in the pit; God's hand shows only later. In the Qur'an, Allah reassures Yusuf right there in the dark, and Yusuf is honored as a prophet.
neighbors.shared: the pit is not the end of your story.

neighbors.heading: the last freedom
neighbors.text: Today Joseph sat in a pit while his brothers ate lunch. The psychiatrist Viktor Frankl survived Nazi camps and wrote about what can't be taken from a person. Everything else can go, he said, but not the freedom to choose your attitude in any circumstances. People who still had a reason, someone or something waiting, often found a way to endure.
neighbors.difference: Genesis says the Lord was with Joseph and turned the evil toward good. Frankl writes as a doctor: meaning is found by the person, even in suffering, and his claim doesn't depend on God.
neighbors.shared: even at the bottom, something in you is still yours.
neighbors.sources: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: he gave his head
neighbors.text: Today two midwives refused a king's order to kill. Sikhs remember a Guru who refused an emperor. When Kashmiri Pandits, Hindus, were pressed to give up their faith, Guru Tegh Bahadur stood up for them. He was executed in Delhi rather than convert. His son, Guru Gobind Singh, wrote that he gave his head, but not his faith.
neighbors.difference: Shiphrah and Puah live, and God gives them households. Guru Tegh Bahadur was not rescued; Sikhs honor his death for the freedom of people of another religion to keep their own.
neighbors.shared: sometimes faith looks like a quiet, brave no.
neighbors.sources: Bachittar Natak, Guru Gobind Singh (paraphrase); Sikh historical tradition

neighbors.heading: the boy who wouldn't stop
neighbors.text: Today two women feared God more than Pharaoh. Hindus tell of Prahlada, whose father, the demon king Hiranyakashipu, demanded to be worshipped. Prahlada kept praying to Vishnu. His father threatened him again and again, and still the boy wouldn't stop. In the end Vishnu burst from a pillar as Narasimha, half man, half lion, to save him.
neighbors.difference: The midwives are saved by a quick answer and quiet courage; God's reward comes after. Prahlada is saved by Vishnu appearing in person, in a form that slipped past every protection his father had.
neighbors.shared: no king's order outranks what's right.

neighbors.heading: drop by drop
neighbors.text: Today Pharaoh hardened his heart, then did it again, and again. The Buddha described that slow build: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the fool becomes full of evil, even if he gather it little by little." The next verse says the same of good: the wise fill up with it, drop by drop.
neighbors.difference: Exodus says Pharaoh hardened his own heart, and later that the LORD hardened it, which readers still wrestle with. In Buddhist teaching no God hardens anyone; our own repeated actions shape the mind.
neighbors.shared: small choices, repeated, become who we are.

neighbors.heading: how habits harden
neighbors.text: Today relief came, and Pharaoh took his word back, again and again. The Catholic Church names this pattern plainly. Its Catechism teaches that sin creates a pull toward more sin: repeat the same act, and it becomes a vice, clouding the conscience until right and wrong are harder to see.
neighbors.difference: Catholics also name a cure: confession, a sacrament where a priest speaks Christ's forgiveness aloud. Many other Christians confess straight to God, without a priest.
neighbors.shared: a hard heart can still be softened.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1865 (paraphrase); Exodus 8:15

neighbors.heading: rich in what you let alone
neighbors.text: Today the manna rotted when people hoarded it. Henry David Thoreau went to live by Walden Pond to find out how little he truly needed. He came back with this: "a man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone." Enough isn't a pile. It's a way of seeing.
neighbors.difference: Manna is a gift from God, gathered fresh each morning in trust. Thoreau's simplicity is a choice a person makes with clear eyes, an experiment in living, without needing anyone to send the bread.
neighbors.shared: enough for today can be enough.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden, "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For"

neighbors.heading: two loaves
neighbors.text: Today God sent bread for one day at a time. Jews remember it every week. Before the sabbath, a double portion fell, so on Shabbat two loaves of challah sit on the table. And the Talmud warns: whoever has bread in the basket and asks, what will I eat tomorrow, is of little faith.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear manna in "give us this day our daily bread," and in Jesus calling himself the bread of life. Jews keep it at their own table, in two loaves under a cloth each Shabbat.
neighbors.shared: trust shows up in how we think about tomorrow's bread.
neighbors.sources: Exodus 16:22; Talmud, Shabbat 117b and Sotah 48b (paraphrase); Matthew 6:11; John 6:35

neighbors.heading: the great vow
