neighbors.text: Today God gave short, blunt rules: don't kill, don't steal, don't lie. Hindus know a short list too. In the Yoga Sutras, Patanjali names five restraints: non-harming, truthfulness, not stealing, sexual restraint, and not grasping. He calls them a great vow, for everyone, no matter their birth, place or time.
neighbors.difference: At Sinai the commandments are God's words in a covenant with a people. Patanjali's restraints are the first step of a yoga path toward a still, clear mind, held as dharma rather than tablets from a mountain.
neighbors.shared: a good life starts with a few simple don'ts.

neighbors.heading: kindness to parents
neighbors.text: Today the second tablet began at home: honor your father and mother. The Qur'an has its own list, and parents come right after God: "Thy Lord hath decreed, that ye worship none save Him, and (that ye show) kindness to parents." The verses go on: don't kill, don't go near adultery, don't touch an orphan's wealth, give full measure.
neighbors.difference: Christians receive the ten words through Moses and hear Jesus sum them up in love of God and neighbor. Muslims receive this list as revelation to Muhammad, part of the Qur'an recited in prayer.
neighbors.shared: honoring your parents is where goodness learns to walk.

neighbors.heading: theirs, not ours
neighbors.text: Today the farmer left the corners of the field for the poor. Catholics keep a line from Pope Saint Gregory the Great: when we give the poor what they need, we aren't handing over what is ours. We're giving back what is theirs. The Church teaches that the goods of the earth are meant for everyone.
neighbors.difference: Catholic teaching gathers this into a long tradition of social teaching from popes and bishops. Other Christians often speak of stewardship and generosity, without one shared body of teaching.
neighbors.shared: some of what you hold was always meant for someone else.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2402 and 2446, quoting Gregory the Great (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: work, then share
neighbors.text: Today the edges of the harvest belonged to the poor. Sikhs are taught to work honestly and share what they earn. Guru Nanak said it in one line: one who eats what he earns by his own work, and gives some of it away, knows the path. Many Sikhs set aside a tenth, dasvandh, for others.
neighbors.difference: Leviticus leaves food in the field for the poor to gather themselves. Sikhs also share it cooked and served: at langar, anyone sits on the floor and eats as an equal.
neighbors.shared: honest work is made whole by sharing it.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak, Var Sarang, Ang 1245 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: more roots than branches
neighbors.text: Today's psalm pictured a person like a tree by rivers of water. The Mishnah grew that tree further. A person whose learning is greater than their deeds is like a tree with many branches and few roots: the wind tips it over. One whose deeds are greater is like a tree with deep roots: every wind in the world can't move it.
neighbors.difference: Christians often read Psalm 1 alongside Jesus' house built on rock. The Mishnah's sage measures it his own way: branches are what you know, roots are what you do, and the roots must win.
neighbors.shared: what you do sinks deeper roots than what you know.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (3:22 in some editions) (paraphrase); Jeremiah 17:8; Matthew 7:24

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today's psalm warned about where you walk, stand and sit, and with whom. Buddhists tell of Ananda, who said to the Buddha: good friendship must be half of the holy life. The Buddha corrected him. Don't say that, he said. Good friends, good companions, are the whole of it.
neighbors.difference: The psalm's happy person delights in God's law day and night. In the Buddha's teaching, a good friend helps you walk the path to freedom from suffering, with no creator God in view.
neighbors.shared: the company you keep shapes what you grow into.

neighbors.heading: don't despair
neighbors.text: Today David's silence dried him out until he told God everything. Muslims turn back too; it's called tawbah, returning. The Qur'an speaks to anyone who has gone wrong: "Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins."
neighbors.difference: Christians hear forgiveness in Psalm 32 and see it fulfilled through Jesus' cross. Muslims turn to Allah directly, with no one between, and the Qur'an says Allah can even change bad deeds into good ones for those who repent.
neighbors.shared: it's never too late to come back.

neighbors.heading: the weight of a secret
neighbors.text: Today the psalm said that holding a wrong inside made the bones ache. Psychologists have studied that weight. James Pennebaker asked people to write about painful things they'd kept to themselves. In his studies, many felt better afterward, and some even needed the doctor less. Putting it into words seemed to set something down.
neighbors.difference: The psalm's relief comes from God, who forgives. Psychology describes the relief of telling, and says nothing about who, if anyone, forgives.
neighbors.shared: what we stop hiding stops weighing us down.
neighbors.sources: James W. Pennebaker, research on expressive writing (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the fish and the water
neighbors.text: Today the psalm longed for God like a deer for water. Guru Nanak used water too. He told his own mind: love the Lord the way a fish loves water. The more water there is, the happier the fish; take it away, and it can't live a moment.
neighbors.difference: The psalmist thirsts from far away, cast down, remembering the temple. For Guru Nanak, the water is the Name, and the longing is met by remembering it, day after day, wherever you are.
neighbors.shared: some thirst is a sign of where we belong.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: like a calf for milk
neighbors.text: Today a deer panted for running water. In a Hindu scripture, a dying warrior named Vritra prays the same ache to Vishnu: like baby birds without wings longing for their mother, like a hungry calf longing for milk, like a lover longing for the beloved far away, so my mind longs to see you, lotus-eyed one.
neighbors.difference: The psalmist longs for the one God of Israel, whom Christians know in Jesus. Vritra longs for Vishnu, seen with lotus eyes; for many Hindus, the one divine is loved in such personal forms.
neighbors.shared: longing for god is a kind of prayer.

items.lessonTitle: Teach us to number our days (Psalm 90)

neighbors.heading: five things to remember
neighbors.text: Today the psalm asked God to teach us to count our days. The Buddha gave five things to remember often: I will grow old. I will get sick. I will die. Everything I love will change, and I will be parted from it. And my actions are what I truly own.
neighbors.difference: The psalm counts our days so God can give us a heart of wisdom and satisfy us with mercy. The Buddha's reflection is meant to loosen clinging and turn us to good action, with no creator asked to help.
neighbors.shared: remembering life is short helps us live it well.

neighbors.heading: dust thou art
neighbors.text: Today the psalm said our lives are like grass. Catholics feel that on their foreheads each Ash Wednesday, when ashes are marked and words from Genesis can be spoken: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." Saint Benedict told his monks to keep death daily before their eyes, so each day would count.
neighbors.difference: Ash Wednesday is kept by Catholics and some other churches. For Catholics the ashes are a sacramental, a blessed sign that opens Lent, while many Christians mark the season without them.
neighbors.shared: counting our days makes each one matter.
neighbors.sources: Genesis 3:19 (Douay-Rheims); Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 4 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: name it to tame it
neighbors.text: Today exiles hung their harps on the willows, and the psalm kept even their rage. Psychologists have noticed that naming a hard feeling can loosen its grip. In Matthew Lieberman's brain studies, putting feelings into words calmed the brain's alarm center. The psalm said its grief out loud instead of performing a happy song.
neighbors.difference: The psalm speaks its grief and anger to God, and readers still struggle with its last lines. Psychology says nothing about who hears; it only finds that naming the feeling helps.
neighbors.shared: sorrow said honestly is easier to carry.
neighbors.sources: Matthew D. Lieberman and colleagues, research on affect labeling (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the broken glass
neighbors.text: Today the exiles vowed: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." Jews still keep that vow. At Jewish weddings, at the height of joy, a glass is broken to remember Jerusalem, and sometimes this very verse is said. Jews pray facing toward Jerusalem, too.
neighbors.difference: Christians often read Jerusalem in the psalm as also the heavenly city, the home Jesus promised. For Jews it is also a real city on a real hill, remembered at weddings and in prayers facing it.
neighbors.shared: even our happiest days can hold room for remembering.

neighbors.heading: the king who kept his word
neighbors.text: Today Job lost everything and still did not curse God. Hindus tell of King Harishchandra, tested by the sage Vishvamitra. To keep a promise, he gave up his kingdom, then was parted from his wife and son, and worked guarding a cremation ground. Through every loss, he would not break his word.
neighbors.difference: Job is tested on whether he'll serve God for nothing. Harishchandra is tested on truth, keeping his word whatever it costs, and in the end the gods restore him for it.
neighbors.shared: goodness that holds when everything's lost is goodness indeed.
neighbors.sources: Markandeya Purana, the story of Harishchandra (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: most merciful
neighbors.text: Today Job sat in the ashes. Muslims know him as the prophet Ayyub. The Qur'an gives his prayer: "Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy." He doesn't demand; he names the pain and names God's mercy. Allah answers, restores him, and says: "Lo! We found him steadfast."
neighbors.difference: The book of Job is long, with friends who argue and a whirlwind that answers. The Qur'an tells Ayyub's story in a few verses and holds him up as a model of patience, sabr.
neighbors.shared: you can tell god it hurts and still trust his mercy.

neighbors.heading: idleness, the enemy
neighbors.text: Today the ant worked with no boss. Saint Benedict wrote in his rule for monks that idleness is the enemy of the soul, so the brothers should spend set hours working with their hands and set hours in holy reading. They are truly monks, he said, when they live by the labor of their hands.
neighbors.difference: Many Christians speak of work as a calling from God. Catholic tradition also sets work inside the rhythm of prayer in its monasteries, and keeps a feast for Saint Joseph the Worker, a carpenter.
neighbors.shared: honest work can be a way of prayer.

neighbors.heading: the carpenter's bread
neighbors.text: Today the ant gathered food in summer. Sikhs tell a story of Guru Nanak in a town called Saidpur. A rich official invited him to a feast; he chose instead to eat with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter. Pressed to explain, the story says, he squeezed the two breads: from Lalo's came milk, from the rich man's, blood.
neighbors.difference: Proverbs praises the ant for working ahead and storing up. Sikhs honor kirat karni, honest work, above all for how it's earned: cleanly, without exploiting anyone, and then shared.
neighbors.shared: bread earned honestly feeds more than the body.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition, Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the first words awake
neighbors.text: Today the poet found God's mercies "new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Many Jews say those last words each morning. Before getting out of bed, eyes barely open, they say Modeh Ani: I thank you, living King, for returning my soul to me with compassion; great is your faithfulness.
neighbors.difference: Christians sing this verse in hymns and hear God's faithfulness fulfilled in Jesus. Jews carry it into the first breath of the day, thanking God for the soul given back after sleep.
neighbors.shared: every morning is a gift handed back to you.
neighbors.sources: Lamentations 3:23; Modeh Ani, the Jewish waking prayer (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: only today
neighbors.text: Today mercy came new each morning, not stored up from yesterday. The Buddha taught a short verse about this one day: don't chase the past, don't lose yourself in the future. The past is gone, the future hasn't come. See what is here, now, clearly, and do today what needs doing.
neighbors.difference: Lamentations rests on God's steady love, renewed each dawn. The Buddha points to the present moment itself, and Buddhists don't look to a creator to renew it.
neighbors.shared: this morning is a fresh place to begin.

neighbors.heading: if they lean toward peace
neighbors.text: Today Isaiah saw swords beaten into plowshares. The Qur'an calls paradise the home of peace: "Allah summoneth to the abode of peace." And facing an enemy, it says: "And if they incline to peace, incline thou also to it, and trust in Allah." Muslims greet each other with peace: as-salamu alaykum.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah sees a day when nations stop learning war. The Qur'an also sets rules for when fighting is allowed, and tells believers to choose peace whenever the other side reaches for it.
neighbors.shared: when someone reaches for peace, reach back.

neighbors.heading: a peace people build
neighbors.text: Today the iron that killed was reforged to feed. The philosopher Immanuel Kant wrote a short book called Perpetual Peace. He argued that lasting peace isn't just a dream: nations could build it, with fair laws at home, a federation of free states, and, in time, an end to standing armies.
neighbors.difference: Isaiah's peace comes when the nations go up to God's mountain to learn his ways. Kant's peace is built by people through reason and agreements, without needing a mountain or a prophet.
neighbors.shared: you can turn what wounds into something that feeds.

neighbors.heading: why search the forest?
neighbors.text: Today God promised to write his law on the heart. Guru Tegh Bahadur asked a gentle question in one of his hymns: why go searching for God in the forest? He lives in everything, always untouched, and he's already with you. Like fragrance in a flower, like a reflection in a mirror, he is within.
neighbors.difference: Jeremiah promises a new covenant on a day to come, which Christians see begun in Jesus. Guru Tegh Bahadur says the Lord is within already; the work is to look, and to remember the Name.
neighbors.shared: what matters most is closer than you think.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Tegh Bahadur, Raag Dhanasari, Ang 684 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seated in every heart
neighbors.text: Today the law moved from stone to the heart. Near the end of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that the Lord dwells in the heart of every being, moving them all. Then he says: take refuge in him with your whole being, and by his grace you will find peace.
neighbors.difference: Jeremiah's promise is a covenant, God writing his teaching on a people's heart. In the Gita, the Lord is already seated within every living being; Hindu schools read that as oneness or as close belonging.
neighbors.shared: the truest teacher may be speaking from inside you.

neighbors.heading: as a mother protects
neighbors.text: Today God held a toddler's arms and bent down to feed him. In a Buddhist teaching on loving-kindness, the Buddha reaches for a parent too: just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so let a person grow a boundless love for every living being.
neighbors.difference: In Hosea, the parent's love comes from God toward his people. In the Metta Sutta, that mother's love is something a person grows in themselves, toward all beings; no God is needed.
neighbors.shared: the best love looks like a parent's care.

neighbors.heading: father, and mother too
neighbors.text: Today God was a parent bending down to feed a child. The Catholic Catechism says God's tenderness can also be pictured as a mother's, though God is beyond both. The English mystic Julian of Norwich, honored by Catholics, wrote it boldly: as truly as God is our Father, so truly is God our Mother.
neighbors.difference: Catholics, like Orthodox Christians, see a mother's care in Mary and ask her prayers; she is not God, but the Church calls her mother. Many other Christians honor Mary without asking her prayers.
neighbors.shared: you were held before you ever noticed.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 239 (paraphrase); Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love, chapter 59 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one word for a life
neighbors.text: Today Micah boiled everything down to three: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Confucius was once asked for one word to guide a whole life. He answered: "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others."
neighbors.difference: Micah's three end with walking humbly with God. Confucius keeps his rule among people, at home and in the town; he spoke little of spirits, and his guide works whether or not you pray.
neighbors.shared: a whole good life can fit in one short line.

neighbors.heading: 613, then three
neighbors.text: Today Micah gave a short answer to a big question. The Talmud noticed. It says Moses received 613 commandments, then prophets came and gathered them into fewer: David into eleven, Isaiah into six, and Micah into three: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with your God.
neighbors.difference: Christians often read Micah 6:8 as a life lived by grace in Christ. In the Talmud, the short lists don't replace the 613; they show the heart of commandments Jews still keep.
neighbors.shared: underneath many rules, a few simple loves.

neighbors.heading: steady in gain and loss
neighbors.text: Today Habakkuk lost figs, grapes, olives, grain and flocks, and still said yet. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to do his work without clinging to how it turns out, the same in success and failure. That evenness of mind, he says, is what yoga is.
neighbors.difference: Krishna teaches a mind that stays steady, unmoved by gain or loss. Habakkuk isn't unmoved: he trembles first, then chooses joy in God anyway, while the loss is still real.
neighbors.shared: peace can stand even when the fields are bare.

neighbors.heading: good either way
neighbors.text: Today Habakkuk rejoiced beside empty stalls. The Prophet Muhammad said something like it: how wonderful is the believer's affair, for all of it is good. If something good comes, he is grateful, and that is good for him. If hardship comes, he is patient, and that is good for him too.
neighbors.difference: Habakkuk speaks from one terrible season, choosing joy in God. The hadith covers both kinds of days and names two answers, gratitude and patience, shukr and sabr.
neighbors.shared: there's a way to stay grateful whatever the harvest.

neighbors.heading: oil for the sick
neighbors.text: Today Jeremiah asked why there was no healing balm. Catholics answer with oil. The letter of James says: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." The Church keeps it as a sacrament, the Anointing of the Sick.
neighbors.difference: Many Christians pray for the sick, and some anoint them. For Catholics this anointing is one of seven sacraments, given by a priest, and they believe Christ himself acts in it to strengthen and heal.
neighbors.shared: no one should face sickness without someone at their side.
neighbors.sources: James 5:14 (Douay-Rheims); Catechism of the Catholic Church 1499–1532 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the medicine of the name
neighbors.text: Today the weeping prophet asked: is there no physician there? Sikhs have a line about medicine in Sukhmani Sahib, a long hymn of peace by Guru Arjan: the Name of God is the medicine for every illness. Many Sikhs recite Sukhmani Sahib when someone is ill or grieving.
neighbors.difference: Jeremiah weeps because the medicine is there and his people aren't healed. For Sikhs, the medicine is remembering the Name, and it's always within reach, whoever you are.
neighbors.shared: there is a balm, even when it's hard to find.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Now let me go in peace (Luke 2:21–35)

neighbors.heading: into his hand
neighbors.text: Today old Simeon held a baby and said he could now go in peace. Jews sing a hymn called Adon Olam, often at the end of prayers and at bedtime. Its last lines put the soul in God's hands: into his hand I place my spirit, when I sleep and when I wake. The LORD is with me; I will not fear.
neighbors.difference: Christians believe Simeon saw the Messiah he'd waited for, in the child Jesus. Judaism still looks ahead to the messianic age, and Jews sing Adon Olam's trust in God in the meantime.
neighbors.shared: you can rest when you know whose hands hold you.
neighbors.sources: Adon Olam, closing lines (paraphrase); Psalm 31:6 (31:5 in KJV)

neighbors.heading: a peaceful last word
neighbors.text: Today Simeon was ready to be relieved of his watch. The Buddha, lying down for the last time at Kusinara, was calm, and his last words were for his students: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!"
neighbors.difference: Simeon's peace comes from seeing the promised child, the salvation God sent. The Buddha's peace comes from seeing that everything changes, and he hands the work to his students rather than to a savior.
neighbors.shared: a life lived well can end in peace.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 16, Maha-parinibbana Sutta, chapter 6 (Rhys Davids)

neighbors.heading: give full measure
neighbors.text: Today John told tax collectors not to cheat and soldiers not to extort. A surah of the Qur'an opens: "Woe unto the defrauders," those who demand full measure for themselves and short-weigh others. And Muslims give zakat, a set share of their wealth each year, for those in need.
neighbors.difference: John gives each crowd a simple, personal answer as they turn back to God. In Islam, zakat is one of the five pillars, a required act of worship with its own fixed share.
neighbors.shared: fair weights and open hands go together.

neighbors.heading: the child in the pond
neighbors.text: Today John said: if you have two coats, give one away. The philosopher Peter Singer asks you to picture a child drowning in a shallow pond. You'd wade in, even if it ruined your shoes. Then he asks: if you can prevent something bad without giving up anything as important, shouldn't you, near or far?
neighbors.difference: John calls people to turn toward God before the one who is coming. Singer argues from reason alone, without appeal to God: there's the person in need, and your coat.
neighbors.shared: if you have more than enough, someone's need is close.

items.lessonTitle: Give, and it will be given (Luke 6:27–38)

neighbors.heading: earn, then share
neighbors.text: Today Jesus pictured a gift pressed down, shaken together and running over. Sikhs build giving into an ordinary day. Guru Nanak taught that the one who eats from honest work and gives some of it away has found the path. Sikhs call it vand chhakna, sharing what you have, and the langar, a free kitchen where anyone can sit and eat, is that sharing with a ladle.
neighbors.difference: Jesus ties giving to God's mercy and a promise: the measure you give comes back to you. For Sikhs, sharing stands beside honest work and remembering God's name, a daily discipline given without counting what returns.
neighbors.shared: an open hand belongs to an ordinary day.
neighbors.sources: Guru Nanak, salok in Raag Sarang, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 1245 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a gift that expects nothing
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said lend, hoping for nothing back. Hindus hear an echo in the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna sorts gifts by the heart behind them. The purest gift, he says, is given simply because giving is right, at the right time and place, to someone who can't pay it back. Hindus call this kind of giving dana.
neighbors.difference: Jesus roots giving in God as a merciful Father: be merciful, as your Father is merciful. In the Gita, a pure gift is part of dharma, doing what's right without craving its fruit.
neighbors.shared: the best gift isn't a trade.

neighbors.heading: a mother and a mustard seed
neighbors.text: Today Jesus saw a widow walking behind her only son's body and was moved deep inside. Buddhists tell of a grieving mother too. Kisa Gotami carried her dead little son from house to house, begging for medicine. The Buddha sent her to find a mustard seed from a home where no one had ever died. She found no such home, and laid her son to rest.
neighbors.difference: In Luke, Jesus stops the funeral and gives the son back to his mother alive. In the Buddhist story the child isn't brought back; the Buddha's compassion helps Kisa Gotami see that loss touches every house, and she seeks freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: no one should have to grieve alone at the gate.
neighbors.sources: the story of Kisa Gotami, Dhammapada Commentary on verse 114 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a mother who stood near
neighbors.text: Today a widow walked behind her only son, and Jesus said, weep not. Catholics carry that picture to Mary at the cross. An old Latin hymn, the Stabat Mater, sings it in English: "At the Cross her station keeping, / Stood the mournful Mother weeping." Catholics honor her as Our Lady of Sorrows, a mother who knows this road.
neighbors.difference: Many Christians remember Mary standing at the cross. Catholics also ask her prayers in their own grief, trusting her as a mother who understands; many Protestant Christians honor her deeply but pray to God alone.
neighbors.shared: the grieving are seen, and someone stays close.
neighbors.sources: Stabat Mater, tr. Edward Caswall (1849) · John 19:25 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a little effort every day
neighbors.text: Today Luke added one word to a hard saying: take up your cross daily. The psychologist William James gave daily advice too. In his chapter on habit he wrote: "Keep the faculty of effort alive in you by a little gratuitous exercise every day." Do something hard just because you'd rather not, he said, so the strength is there when a real test comes.
neighbors.difference: For James, small daily effort trains your own will and character. Luke's daily cross means following Jesus and letting go of self for his sake, even toward suffering, and Christians trust God's grace to carry them, not willpower alone.
neighbors.shared: the big yes is built out of small daily ones.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. 4, "Habit"

neighbors.heading: a yoke every morning
neighbors.text: Today Jesus asked for a cross taken up daily, not once. Jews take something up daily too. In traditional prayer, morning and evening, Jews say the Shema, which tells them to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." The Mishnah calls saying it accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven: a bond with God, renewed each day.
neighbors.difference: Jesus' daily cross means following him, even toward suffering. The Shema declares that God is one and binds a Jew to God's commandments through the Torah and the covenant, not through Jesus.
neighbors.shared: faith is a thing you pick up again each morning.

neighbors.heading: a dawn prayer for light
neighbors.text: Today the disciples asked, teach us to pray, and Jesus gave them a short prayer to keep. Hindus keep a short prayer too: the Gayatri mantra from the Rig Veda, handed from teacher to student and often chanted at dawn. It turns toward the divine light of Savitr and asks, in plural words, that this light brighten and stir our minds.
neighbors.difference: Jesus teaches his friends to call God Father and ask for bread, forgiveness and protection. The Gayatri turns to the divine as the radiant source of light, Savitr, and asks for one thing: a mind lit from within.
neighbors.shared: a few words, said daily, can hold a whole life.

neighbors.heading: the opening
neighbors.text: Today Jesus' friends asked, teach us to pray. Muslims learn a prayer they recite in every unit of the daily prayers: Al-Fatiha, the Opening. Its heart asks in plural words: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help. Show us the straight path." Even a Muslim praying alone says we.
neighbors.difference: Jesus teaches his followers to call God Father. Islam doesn't call God Father; Al-Fatiha praises God as Lord of the Worlds, the Beneficent, the Merciful, and Muslims pray it in Arabic, in the Qur'an's own words.
neighbors.shared: even alone, a prayer can say "we."

neighbors.heading: God as a mother
neighbors.text: Today Jesus pictured himself as a hen, gathering her chicks under her wings. A Catholic mystic took that picture further. Julian of Norwich, who lived enclosed in a small cell beside an English church, wrote: "As verily as God is our Father, so verily God is our Mother." She saw Christ's love as a mother's: feeding, carrying, never letting go.
neighbors.difference: Jesus uses the hen picture in a lament over Jerusalem. Julian builds a whole meditation on Christ's motherly love; the Church reads her as one mystic's vision, treasured and taught, while still praying to God as Father, the name Jesus taught.
neighbors.shared: love that covers you is strong, not soft.
neighbors.sources: Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love, ch. 59 (Warrack 1901)

neighbors.heading: you are my mother
neighbors.text: Today Jesus pictured himself as a mother hen, wings spread over her chicks. Sikhs sing to God as mother and father both. Guru Arjan wrote, in words often sung: you are my father, you are my mother; you are my kin and my brother. In Gurbani, the soul runs to God like a child, sheltered, fed and unafraid.
neighbors.difference: Jesus speaks of gathering Jerusalem himself, the one who would die for her. For Sikhs, God is one and formless, never born as a person, and mother and father are love-names for that one God.
neighbors.shared: everyone needs somewhere to run when the hawk is overhead.
neighbors.sources: Guru Arjan, Raag Majh, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 103 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: come back as far as you can
neighbors.text: Today a father saw his son a great way off, and ran. Jews tell a parable too. A king's son had wandered far. The king sent word: come back to me. The son answered, I can't, it's too far. The king sent again: come back as far as you can, and I will come the rest of the way. Jews call that turning home teshuvah.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, Jesus tells the story, and the father's welcome is God's grace made known in him. In Jewish teaching, teshuvah needs no go-between: the one who turns comes straight to God, who calls Israel home through the Torah and the prophets.
neighbors.shared: the road home is shorter than it looks from far away.

neighbors.heading: the poor son who came home
neighbors.text: Today a son came home rehearsing a servant's speech. Buddhists tell a parable of a wandering son too. In the Lotus Sutra, a rich man's son leaves, drifts poor for years, and stumbles back to his father's gate, too frightened to believe he belongs. The father hires him for humble work and draws him close, step by step, until he can hear: all of this is yours.
neighbors.difference: Luke's father runs and restores his son at once, with a robe and a ring. In the Lotus Sutra the father stands for the Buddha, leading gently by stages, and the inheritance is the son's own capacity to awaken.
neighbors.shared: you belong in the house before you believe you do.

neighbors.heading: the one who remembered
neighbors.text: Today one healed man in ten came back to say thank you. Muslims tell a story of three: a leper, a bald man and a blind man. An angel healed each one and gave them wealth. Later he came back as a poor traveler asking for help. Two said their riches were simply theirs. Only the once-blind man gave freely, remembering who had healed him.
neighbors.difference: In Luke, the Samaritan's thanks is given at Jesus' feet. In the hadith, the healing came from God alone; the angel is only a messenger, and the Qur'an promises that God gives more to those who give thanks.
neighbors.shared: thank you is the shortest way back to where the gift came from.

neighbors.heading: counting blessings
neighbors.text: Today nine walked on healed, and one turned back to give thanks. Psychologists have tested what turning back does. In one study, Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough asked people to jot down a few things they were grateful for each week. Compared with people who listed hassles, they felt better about their lives as a whole. Noticing the gift seems to change the one who notices.
neighbors.difference: In psychology, gratitude is a habit that helps the person who practices it, whoever it's aimed at. For Christians, thanks has an address: the Samaritan turns back to Jesus and glorifies God.
neighbors.shared: noticing a gift changes the one who notices.
neighbors.sources: Emmons & McCullough, "Counting Blessings Versus Burdens," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (2003) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the carpenter's bread
neighbors.text: Today a widow's two tiny coins counted for more than all. Sikhs tell a story of Guru Nanak. Invited to a feast by Malik Bhago, a rich official, he chose instead the plain bread of Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter. Tradition says that when he squeezed both breads, milk came from Lalo's, earned honestly, and blood from Bhago's, earned by crushing the poor.
neighbors.difference: Jesus measures the widow's gift by what she had left: nothing. The Sikh story measures bread by how it was earned, honest work against exploitation, which is why Sikhs prize kirat karni, earning an honest living.
neighbors.shared: a small gift from a clean heart outweighs the plaque.
neighbors.sources: the Janamsakhis, traditional lives of Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a leaf, a flower, a handful of rice
neighbors.text: Today Jesus watched a widow give two tiny coins and called it more than all. Hindus hear Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita: whoever offers me with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, I accept it. And they tell of poor Sudama, who brought his old friend Krishna only a handful of beaten rice, and Krishna ate it with joy.
neighbors.difference: The widow gives to the temple treasury, and Jesus notices what her gift costs her. In the Gita, Krishna himself receives the offering, and what makes it precious is the love it carries, not its size or its cost.
neighbors.shared: love can't be weighed by what's in the hand.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 9.26 (paraphrase) · Bhagavata Purana, book 10, the story of Sudama (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: hatred ends with love
neighbors.text: Today, with swords out in the dark, Jesus said enough, and healed the ear of a man who'd come to arrest him. Buddhists keep a verse from the Dhammapada close: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." A sword answered with a sword only keeps the wheel turning.
neighbors.difference: Jesus heals as the one about to suffer, and Christians see God's own love at work in him. The Dhammapada names a law of the mind: letting go of hatred frees the one who lets go, a path walked with the Buddha as teacher.
neighbors.shared: someone has to be the first to put the sword down.

neighbors.heading: a soldier who stopped
neighbors.text: Today Jesus stopped a sword and healed the wound it made. Catholics remember Saint Martin of Tours, a Roman soldier. His early biographer says Martin told the emperor he was Christ's soldier now and could not fight. Called a coward, he offered to stand unarmed at the front of the battle line, with only the sign of the cross.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear Jesus' "no more" in different ways; some, like many Quakers and Mennonites, refuse to take up arms. The Catholic Church honors Martin as a saint and also teaches that defending others can be just, under strict conditions and only as a last resort.
neighbors.shared: you can still heal a wound on the other side.
neighbors.sources: Sulpicius Severus, Life of Saint Martin, ch. 4 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2309 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: they don't know
neighbors.text: Today Jesus prayed for the men crucifying him: they know not what they do. The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius began his mornings expecting to meet people who'd be ungrateful and unkind, and reminded himself they act that way because they don't know what is truly good. Seeing that, he wrote, he couldn't be angry with his own kin.
neighbors.difference: Marcus forgives to keep his own mind clear and to keep working beside others as fellow humans. Jesus asks God as Father to forgive his killers, and Christians believe his death opens that forgiveness to the world.
neighbors.shared: seeing someone's blindness can soften your own anger.

neighbors.heading: forgiving before sleep
neighbors.text: Today Jesus forgave the people hurting him while they were still doing it. Jewish prayer books hold a nightly forgiveness. Before the bedtime Shema comes a prayer that says, in short: master of the universe, I forgive anyone who angered or wronged me, in body, in money or in honor, and may no one be punished because of me. Then comes sleep.
neighbors.difference: Jesus forgives his executioners from the cross. Jewish teaching also holds that a wrong against a person isn't wiped away even on Yom Kippur until the wrongdoer makes peace with that person; forgiving and repairing go together.
neighbors.shared: you can set down a grudge before you set down your head.
neighbors.sources: the bedtime Shema, traditional siddur (paraphrase) · Mishnah Yoma 8:9 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Known in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:13–35)

neighbors.heading: the guest is God
neighbors.text: Today two travelers pressed a stranger to stay, because it was toward evening, and at their table they knew him. Hindus learn an old line from the Taittiriya Upanishad: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be to you as a god. In that spirit, many Hindu homes offer a guest water, food and the best seat, as if the divine had walked in.
neighbors.difference: At Emmaus the guest really is the risen Jesus, and Christians meet him again in the breaking of bread. For Hindus, honoring the guest as divine is a way of honoring the divine present in whoever comes to the door.
neighbors.shared: the stranger at your table may be the blessing.

neighbors.heading: Abraham's honored guests
neighbors.text: Today two disciples asked a stranger to stay, and knew him when he broke the bread. Muslims tell of Abraham's guests. The Qur'an says strangers came to him with a greeting of peace; he hurried to his household and brought a fatted calf, and only later learned they were angels. The Prophet taught: whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest.
neighbors.difference: At Emmaus, Christians see the risen Jesus himself in the guest's seat. In Islam, the guests are angels sent by God, Abraham is a prophet, and hospitality is a duty of faith, not a meeting with God in human form.
neighbors.shared: keep a place at the table for whoever's walking by.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 51:24–27 (paraphrase) · hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: born of water
neighbors.text: Today Jesus told Nicodemus about a birth from above, of water and the Spirit. Catholics hear baptism in those words. The Douay-Rheims reads: "unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." The Church calls baptism a new birth, and pours its water over babies as well as grown-ups.
neighbors.difference: Many evangelical Christians hear born again as a moment of personal conversion, often as adults. Catholics, like the Orthodox and many other churches, tie the new birth to baptism itself, a gift that can come before a child is able to choose it.
neighbors.shared: new life can come quietly, like wind you hear but can't hold.
neighbors.sources: John 3:5 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1213 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a new family
neighbors.text: Today Jesus spoke of being born a second time, from above. Sikhs speak of a new birth too. At the Amrit ceremony, initiates drink sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword while prayers are recited. They are told that their father is now Guru Gobind Singh, their mother Mata Sahib Kaur, and their home Anandpur. They become part of the Khalsa.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the new birth comes from God's Spirit through Jesus, and in many churches through baptism. For Sikhs, Amrit is a commitment to the Guru's way, the five Ks and a disciplined life, taken by choice when a person is ready.
neighbors.shared: some beginnings come after you thought you'd already begun.
neighbors.sources: Sikh Rehat Maryada, the Amrit ceremony (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: for Thou art with me
neighbors.text: Today the disciples rowed in the dark until a voice said, it is I; be not afraid. Jews have long carried a psalm into dark places: "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me." There's no promise the valley disappears. Only that the one walking isn't alone in it.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear "it is I" as Jesus himself coming over the water, and some hear the divine name in it. In the psalm, the one who is near is God, the shepherd of Israel, with no one standing in between.
neighbors.shared: fear gets smaller when someone you trust is in the boat.

neighbors.heading: remember, and fear passes
neighbors.text: Today, out on a dark lake, a voice said, be not afraid. The Buddha gave his monks words for fear too. In the sutta of the banner, he said: when you're alone in the forest and fear rises, recall the Buddha, the teaching and the community, and the fear will pass, the way, he said, the gods in battle steadied themselves at the sight of their king's banner.
neighbors.difference: In John, Jesus himself comes across the water to his friends. In the Buddhist teaching, the Buddha isn't arriving to rescue anyone; recalling his qualities steadies the mind from within, so the monk can face the fear.
neighbors.shared: in the dark, it helps to remember who you belong to.

neighbors.heading: light upon light
neighbors.text: Today, in the temple, Jesus said, I am the light of the world. Muslims treasure the Verse of Light: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The similitude of His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp. The lamp is in a glass. The glass is as it were a shining star."
neighbors.difference: Christians hear Jesus naming himself the light. In Islam, the Light is God alone; Jesus is honored as a prophet and messenger, and the verse says God guides to His light whom He will.
neighbors.shared: night still comes, and there's still a lamp.

neighbors.heading: out of the cave
neighbors.text: Today Jesus promised the light of life to anyone who follows. Philosophers have their own story of light. In Plato's Republic, prisoners in a cave take shadows on a wall for the whole world. One is freed and climbs into the sun, and at first the light hurts his eyes. Slowly he sees things as they are, then goes back down to tell the others.
neighbors.difference: For Plato, the light is the Good and the truth, reached by a long climb of the mind. For Christians, the light is a person who comes to people in the dark and says, follow me.
neighbors.shared: the light is worth the climb, and worth going back to share.

neighbors.heading: ointment for the eyes
neighbors.text: Today Jesus put clay on a blind man's eyes and said, go, wash. Sikhs sing of eyes opened too. In the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan writes that the Guru gave the ointment of spiritual wisdom, and the darkness of ignorance was dispelled. For Sikhs, the Guru's word is that ointment: it lets a person see God everywhere.
neighbors.difference: In John, a man blind from birth gets his physical sight back, a sign of who Jesus is. In the Sikh hymn, the blindness is ignorance, and the Guru's word heals the inner eye.
neighbors.shared: sometimes a gentle touch is how we finally see.
neighbors.sources: Guru Arjan, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 293 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the guru's salve
neighbors.text: Today Jesus made clay and anointed a blind man's eyes. Many Hindus greet their teachers with an old verse, found in the Guru Gita, using the very same picture: salutations to the guru, who opened the eyes of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance with the salve of knowledge. For Hindus, the guru is the one who helps you see.
neighbors.difference: Jesus heals a man's actual eyes, and refuses to blame him or his parents for the blindness. In the verse, the darkness is ignorance of the true Self, and the guru's knowledge is what lets a person finally see.
neighbors.shared: a good teacher helps you see for yourself.
neighbors.sources: Guru Gita, the verse in praise of the guru (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: He loved them to the end (John 13:1–17)

neighbors.heading: whoever would tend me
neighbors.text: Today Jesus tied on a towel and washed his friends' dusty feet. Buddhists tell of a monk lying sick and soiled, left alone by the others. The Buddha and Ananda washed him with their own hands and laid him on a bed. Then the Buddha told the monks: whoever would tend me, let him tend the sick.
neighbors.difference: Jesus washes feet as a sign of his love and of the cleansing he gives, and tells his friends to do the same for one another. The Buddha tends the sick monk as a teacher, showing that caring for each other belongs to the path.
neighbors.shared: the humblest work can be the holiest.

neighbors.heading: the mandatum
neighbors.text: Today Jesus washed his disciples' feet and said, I have given you an example. Catholics act it out on Holy Thursday. At the evening Mass of the Lord's Supper, the Roman Missal includes a rite where the priest kneels with a basin and towel and washes the feet of people from the parish. It's called the mandatum, from Jesus' new commandment that night.
neighbors.difference: Many churches read this passage on the Thursday before Easter, and some wash feet too. Catholics also remember that night as the institution of the Eucharist and the priesthood, so the priest kneels as a servant, the way Christ did.
neighbors.shared: love gets down on its knees with a towel.
neighbors.sources: John 13:14–15 (paraphrase) · Roman Missal, Holy Thursday, the Washing of Feet (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: another self
neighbors.text: Today Jesus told his followers, I have called you friends. Aristotle thought hard about friendship. In the Nicomachean Ethics he says the best friends wish each other good for the other's own sake, not for use or for pleasure, and that a good friend is another self. Such friendships are rare, he says, and take time: you have to have eaten salt together.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle's best friendship is between equals in goodness, who grow alike. Jesus calls friends people who aren't his equals, lets them in on all he has heard from the Father, and says the greatest love lays down its life.
neighbors.shared: a friend is someone you let in on the plan.

neighbors.heading: knit soul to soul
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said there's no greater love than laying down your life for your friends. Jews tell of David and Jonathan. The Bible says "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Jonathan, a king's son, risked his father's fury and his own crown to keep his friend alive.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, Jesus' words point toward his own death for his friends, which they believe opens friendship with God to everyone. Jonathan's love is a human friendship, held up by the rabbis as love that depends on nothing in return.
neighbors.shared: a true friend is worth risking something for.
neighbors.sources: 1 Samuel 18:1 (KJV) · Pirkei Avot 5:16, on love that depends on nothing (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: truth alone wins
neighbors.text: Today Pilate asked, what is truth? and walked out before the answer. Hindus keep an old answer from the Mundaka Upanishad: satyam eva jayate, truth alone triumphs, not falsehood. The Upanishad goes on to say the path to the divine is laid with truth, the path the sages walk once their cravings are stilled.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, truth is finally a person: Jesus says he came to bear witness to the truth, and elsewhere, I am the truth. In the Upanishad, truth is the reality beneath everything, and the seeker walks toward it.
neighbors.shared: a big question deserves someone who'll stay for the answer.

neighbors.heading: the Truth is a name
neighbors.text: Today Pilate asked, what is truth? and didn't stay to hear. Muslims count al-Haqq, the Truth, among the names of God. The Qur'an says: "That is because Allah, He is the True." In Islam, truth isn't only a fact to look up; it belongs to God, and every true thing points back to Him.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear Jesus say he bears witness to the truth, and believe he is the truth in person. Muslims honor Jesus as a prophet who spoke the truth, and keep the name al-Haqq for God alone.
neighbors.shared: truth is worth staying in the room for.

neighbors.heading: "I thirst"
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said, I thirst, and soon after, it is finished. A Catholic saint built her life around those two words. Mother Teresa of Calcutta heard in them Jesus' thirst for love, and for the poorest. In the chapels of her Missionaries of Charity, "I thirst" is written on the wall beside the crucifix. Catholics now honor her as Saint Teresa of Calcutta.
neighbors.difference: Christians read "I thirst" first as real thirst, and as scripture fulfilled. Catholics, with Teresa, also hear in it Christ's longing for each person, and answer it by serving him in the dying and the poor.
neighbors.shared: a cup of water can answer a cry.
neighbors.sources: John 19:28 · writings of Saint Teresa of Calcutta (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: water for both sides
neighbors.text: Today, from the cross, Jesus said, I thirst, and someone lifted up a sponge. Sikhs remember Bhai Kanhaiya, who carried water to wounded soldiers on the battlefield, his own side and the enemy's. When others complained to Guru Gobind Singh, Bhai Kanhaiya said he saw no enemy, only the Guru's light in every face. The Guru gave him ointment too, to tend their wounds.
neighbors.difference: John hears Jesus' thirst as scripture fulfilled while he finishes his work on the cross. Bhai Kanhaiya's story is about seva, selfless service, given to anyone in need because God's light is in all.
neighbors.shared: thirst is thirst, whatever side you're on.
neighbors.sources: the Sikh tradition of Bhai Kanhaiya (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: John close: all the books in the world (John 21:20–25)

neighbors.heading: if the sky were parchment
neighbors.text: Today John ended his Gospel saying the world itself couldn't hold all the books. Many Jews, in Ashkenazi synagogues, sing something like it on Shavuot, in an old Aramaic hymn called Akdamut: if the heavens were parchment, every reed a pen, the seas ink and every person a scribe, it still wouldn't be enough to write God's glory.
neighbors.difference: John's overflow is about what Jesus did, too much to write down. Akdamut's is about God's greatness, and it's sung at Shavuot, the feast of receiving the Torah, a book Jews read again and again without end.
neighbors.shared: some stories are bigger than any page can hold.

neighbors.heading: a handful of leaves
neighbors.text: Today John said the world couldn't hold the books if everything Jesus did were written down. The Buddha once picked up a few leaves in a forest and asked his monks: which are more, these in my hand or those overhead? Those overhead, they said. So too, he said, what I know is far more than what I've taught. I teach what leads to the end of suffering.
neighbors.difference: John leaves things out because the story of Jesus is too large to tell. The Buddha leaves things out on purpose, because they don't help a person walk toward the end of suffering.
neighbors.shared: what you need for today fits in one hand.

neighbors.heading: preferring others
neighbors.text: Today Paul wrote: let each esteem other better than themselves. Muslims remember the Ansar of Medina, who welcomed the Prophet's companions when they arrived with nothing. The Qur'an praises them, for they "prefer (the fugitives) above themselves though poverty become their lot." They shared homes and harvests with people they had only just met.
neighbors.difference: Paul roots humility in Christ, who emptied himself to serve. The Qur'an praises the Ansar's generosity as faith in God lived out, with the Prophet as their example.
neighbors.shared: making room for someone is a way of honoring them.

neighbors.heading: live for your neighbor
neighbors.text: Today Paul asked his friends to look not only to their own interests, but to others'. The Stoic philosopher Seneca, in his letters to a friend, said something close: "you must live for your neighbour, if you would live for yourself." A life that turns everything into a question of its own advantage, he thought, can't be a happy one.
neighbors.difference: For Seneca, living for others is what reason and nature ask of a human being, and it makes a good life. Paul roots it in Christ, who came down to serve, and in a shared life in the Spirit.
neighbors.shared: your life gets bigger when it faces outward.

neighbors.heading: contentment is the thread
neighbors.text: Today Paul wrote that he had learned to be content with little or with plenty. Sikhs call contentment santokh. The Japji retells an old picture of a bull holding up the earth: the bull is dharma, born of compassion, and it's contentment that holds everything in place. For Sikhs, santokh grows by remembering God's name.
neighbors.difference: Paul's contentment rests on Christ: I can do all things through him. Sikhs grow santokh by remembering God's name and accepting the hukam, God's will, while still working honestly and standing up for what's right.
neighbors.shared: enough is a place you can learn to live.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauri 16, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 3 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: santosha
neighbors.text: Today Paul said he'd learned the secret of being content, hungry or full. Hindus find contentment in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, where santosha is one of the personal disciplines. The sutra makes a big promise for it: from contentment comes unsurpassed happiness. Not having everything, but not being run by wanting more.
neighbors.difference: Paul's contentment is a secret he was let into, resting on Christ's strength. In the Yoga Sutras, santosha is a practice of the mind, grown alongside other disciplines, that quiets craving on the way to inner freedom.
neighbors.shared: the secret of enough can be learned.

neighbors.heading: a bubble, a mirage
neighbors.text: Today James said a life is a vapor, here a little while and then gone. Buddhists have a verse for it in the Dhammapada: look on the world as a bubble, look on it as a mirage. For Buddhists, seeing that everything passes, anicca, loosens the grip of craving and fear, and makes each passing moment easier to meet.
neighbors.difference: James wants plans held loosely because God holds tomorrow: if the Lord will. The Buddha teaches impermanence as a truth to see clearly for yourself, with no creator God holding the future.
neighbors.shared: hold your plans with an open hand.

neighbors.heading: remember, you are dust
neighbors.text: Today James called a life a vapor that appears for a little time. Catholics put that on their foreheads. On Ash Wednesday, ashes are traced in a cross, often with words from Genesis: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." Then Lent begins: forty days to pray, fast and give, while there's still time.
neighbors.difference: Many Christians mark Ash Wednesday too, and others simply hear James's words. Catholics build the reminder into their year, with ashes, Lent and prayers for the dead, always held inside the hope of the resurrection.
neighbors.shared: a short life can still be lived on purpose.

items.lessonTitle: In deed and in truth (1 John 3:11–18)

neighbors.heading: we become what we do
neighbors.text: Today the letter said, love not in word only, but in deed. Aristotle made a similar point about character. In the Nicomachean Ethics he says we become just by doing just acts, and brave by doing brave ones, the way a builder becomes a builder by building. Good intentions don't make the habit; practice does.
neighbors.difference: For Aristotle, virtue is a human excellence built through practice. First John says love starts with God, who loved first, and the deed is how that love shows up in us, especially for someone in need.
neighbors.shared: love is warmest when it arrives with soup.

neighbors.heading: say little, do much
neighbors.text: Today First John asked for love in deed, not just in word. Jewish teachers said it in their own short way. In Pirkei Avot, Shammai teaches: say little and do much. Shimon, son of Rabban Gamaliel, adds that the main thing isn't study, but doing. And deeds of loving-kindness, gemilut chasadim, are one of three things the world stands on.
neighbors.difference: First John measures love by the cross: Jesus laid down his life, so we love in deed. In Jewish teaching, deeds of kindness are part of the Torah's way and the covenant, done because God asks it and the world needs it.
neighbors.shared: a kindness counts most when it actually shows up.

neighbors.heading: love as the way
neighbors.text: Today the letter said, God is love, and whoever loves is born of God. Hindus who walk the path of bhakti, devotion, speak of love as the way to God. The Narada Bhakti Sutra describes bhakti as supreme love for God, and in the Gita, Krishna says it's by loving devotion that a person truly comes to know him.
neighbors.difference: First John says love begins on God's side: God loved first and sent his Son. In bhakti, love is the devotee's road toward God, often toward Krishna or another form of the divine, and grace meets them there.
neighbors.shared: love isn't only a feeling; it's a road.

neighbors.heading: the Loving
neighbors.text: Today the letter said, God is love. Muslims call God al-Wadud, the Loving, one of His names in the Qur'an: "And He is the Forgiving, the Loving." Another verse speaks of a people whom God loves and who love Him. For Muslims, love begins with God and returns to Him.
neighbors.difference: First John says God is love and showed it by sending his Son. In Islam, the Loving is one of God's beautiful names; His love reaches people through mercy and revelation, and Islam teaches that God has no son.
neighbors.shared: love begins before we ever think to ask for it.

neighbors.heading: to know the book
neighbors.text: Today was about how to keep reading the Bible on your own. Catholics often quote Saint Jerome, who translated it into Latin: ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ. The Second Vatican Council repeated his words and urged believers to read often, with prayer, so that reading becomes a conversation between God and the reader.
neighbors.difference: Christians across many churches keep the Bible open. Catholics read it alongside the Church's tradition and teaching, with a lectionary that walks the whole Church through it together, and in a Bible that holds a few books many Protestant Bibles leave out.
neighbors.shared: a book read slowly, with others, keeps opening.

neighbors.heading: a slow, whole reading
neighbors.text: Today was about reading on your own, a little at a time. Sikhs have a word for that: sehaj path, a slow reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, from the first Ang to the last, at whatever pace a home can keep. When the reading is finished, family and friends gather to give thanks.
neighbors.difference: Christians read the Bible as God's word, written down by many hands. Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib as their living Guru, given a place of honor and carried with care, so reading it is sitting with the Guru.
neighbors.shared: a few pages a day can carry you through the whole book.
neighbors.sources: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on sehaj path (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: your people, my people
neighbors.text: Today Ruth wouldn't let Naomi walk home alone: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Jews read her story aloud on Shavuot, the feast of receiving the Torah. The rabbis heard in her words the shape of someone joining the Jewish people, and drew lessons for welcoming a convert from this very road out of Moab.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, Ruth's line also leads to Jesus, and Matthew names her in his family tree. For Jews, she is King David's great-grandmother and the model of a sincere convert, welcomed as fully Jewish.
neighbors.shared: love can make a stranger family.

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today Ruth held fast to Naomi, a young widow choosing an old one with nothing to give. Buddhists honor that kind of companion too. Once Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, guessed that good friendship was half of the holy life. The Buddha answered: not half. Admirable friendship, good companionship, is the whole of it.
neighbors.difference: Ruth binds herself to Naomi's people and Naomi's God, for life and into the grave. The Buddha's good friend is a companion on the path to freedom from suffering, with no vow to a people or a God.
neighbors.shared: the right friend beside you changes the whole road.

items.lessonTitle: The Lord looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:1–13)

neighbors.heading: where God looks
neighbors.text: Today Samuel admired a tall son, and God said: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." Muslims treasure words very close to it. The Qur'an says: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." And the Prophet Muhammad taught that God looks not at your faces or your wealth, but at your hearts and deeds.
neighbors.difference: In Samuel's story, God looks past appearances to choose one young shepherd as king. In Islam the teaching is a mirror for everyone: no nation, tribe or wealth makes anyone nobler; only the heart, and what it does.
neighbors.shared: you are more than what anyone sees from across a room.

neighbors.heading: worth that shines from inside
neighbors.text: Today the youngest son, out with the sheep, was the one God chose, because God looks on the heart. Philosophers have searched for that inner worth too. Immanuel Kant wrote that nothing is good without condition except a good will. Even if it achieved nothing at all, he said, it would still shine like a jewel, by its own light.
neighbors.difference: In Samuel, the one who sees the heart is God, and the seeing ends in a calling. For Kant, the worth of a good will stands on its own, something reason can recognize whether or not anyone is watching.
neighbors.shared: what's truest about you is something height and looks can't measure.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, section 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the song that steadies
neighbors.text: Today a boy's harp let a tormented king breathe again. For Sikhs, song sits at the center of worship. Guru Nanak traveled with his companion Mardana, who played the rabab while the Guru sang. The Guru Granth Sahib is largely arranged by raag, musical measures, and it calls kirtan, singing God's praise, the highest practice in this dark age.
neighbors.difference: David plays for one troubled man, and the text calls it refreshment, not worship. In a gurdwara, kirtan is worship itself: the Gurus' hymns sung to the congregation, so the word and the music arrive together.
neighbors.shared: music can reach a place that words alone can't.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1075 (paraphrase) · janamsakhi accounts of Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the veda of song
neighbors.text: Today David played, and Saul "was refreshed, and was well." Hindus have long honored sacred sound. One of the Vedas, the Sama Veda, is the Veda of song, its verses set to melody. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that among the Vedas, he is the Sama Veda. Bhajans and kirtan still fill homes and temples with sung devotion.
neighbors.difference: For Saul, music is a gift that eases his suffering for a time. Many Hindus hear sacred sound itself as holy: Krishna names himself in the Veda of song, so singing can be a way of meeting God.
neighbors.shared: a song can carry someone through hours they can't carry themselves.

neighbors.heading: better than a kingdom
neighbors.text: Today God said, "Ask what I shall give thee," and young Solomon chose an understanding heart over riches and long life. Buddhists prize that choice too. The Dhammapada says the first real step on the path is worth more than ruling the whole earth, more than going to heaven. Wisdom, in Buddhism, means seeing things as they truly are.
neighbors.difference: Solomon receives wisdom as a gift from God, asked for in prayer. In much Buddhist teaching, wisdom is grown rather than granted: practiced through mindfulness and meditation until a person sees clearly for themselves.
neighbors.shared: the best thing to ask for is a clearer heart.

neighbors.heading: i preferred her before thrones
neighbors.text: Today Solomon asked for an understanding heart. Catholic Bibles carry a book that answers in his voice, the Book of Wisdom: "Wherefore I wished, and understanding was given me: and I called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came upon me." The Church names wisdom first among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.
neighbors.difference: Most Protestant Bibles leave out the Book of Wisdom, though some still read it as wise writing. Catholics and Orthodox count it as scripture, and Catholics see wisdom as a gift the Holy Spirit gives every believer, not only kings.
neighbors.shared: anyone can ask for a heart that listens.
neighbors.sources: Wisdom 7:7 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1831 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: first, the body
neighbors.text: Today an angel told the exhausted Elijah only this: "Arise and eat." No lecture, just bread and sleep. Psychologists say something similar. Abraham Maslow described human needs in layers: food, water and rest first, then safety, then belonging, and, as a rule, only then the higher reaches of the self. A starving, sleepless mind struggles to hear anything bigger.
neighbors.difference: In Kings, the care comes from God's messenger, and the bread leads to a meeting with God on the mountain. Maslow describes these needs as plain human nature, studied rather than sent; what waits on the mountain is left to each person.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the bravest next step is a meal and a long sleep.
neighbors.sources: 1 Kings 19:5 (KJV) · Abraham Maslow, "A Theory of Human Motivation" (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a healthy body, a way to God
neighbors.text: Today Elijah had to eat and sleep before he could go on. Jewish teaching takes the body just as seriously. Moses Maimonides, rabbi and doctor, wrote that keeping the body healthy is among the ways of God, because a person can't understand or know the Creator while sick. And Shabbat rest isn't a reward. It's a commandment.
neighbors.difference: Elijah's rest is a rescue in a crisis, brought by an angel. In Judaism, care for the body is ongoing: daily habits Maimonides spells out, and a whole day of rest every week, built in before anyone collapses.
neighbors.shared: taking care of your body can be part of faithfulness.
neighbors.sources: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:1 (paraphrase) · Exodus 20:8–10 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the river that washes
neighbors.text: Today a proud general dipped seven times in a plain river and came up clean. Hindus know the holiness of washing in rivers. Pilgrims bathe in the Ganga, praying to be made pure. An old hymn of the Rig Veda asks the Waters to carry away whatever wrong a person has done: a lie, a false oath, a harm.
neighbors.difference: Naaman's healing comes from God through a prophet's word, and the Jordan is plain water. For many Hindus, the Ganga is herself a goddess, Mother Ganga, and bathing in her is devotion as well as cleansing.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the way to be new is as simple as water.

neighbors.heading: washed before you stand
neighbors.text: Today Naaman almost refused a cure because it was too simple: "Wash, and be clean." Muslims wash before prayer, face, hands, head and feet, as the Qur'an teaches. And the Prophet Muhammad said that when a believer washes, the wrongs of the eyes and the hands go out with the water, until they come away clean.
neighbors.difference: Naaman's washing happened once, for a healing, and he had to swallow his pride to do it. Wudu is daily and ordinary: it doesn't heal the body, it prepares a person to stand before God in prayer.
neighbors.shared: a small, humble act can open the door to something holy.

neighbors.heading: the work of their hands
neighbors.text: Today Paul sewed tents in Corinth so the message wouldn't come with a bill. Catholics honor that kind of work too. The Rule of Benedict says monks are truly monks when they live by the labor of their hands, as the apostles did. And the Church keeps a feast of Saint Joseph the Worker, the carpenter, on May 1.
neighbors.difference: Many Christians honor work as Paul did, a way to serve without being a burden. Catholic teaching also calls human work a sharing in God's own work of creation, and gives workers a patron in Joseph.
neighbors.shared: honest work can be a quiet kind of prayer.
neighbors.sources: Rule of Saint Benedict 48 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2427 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: earn honestly, share
neighbors.text: Today Paul worked with his hands so he wouldn't be a burden to anyone. Sikhs make that a way of life: kirat karni, earning an honest living. Guru Nanak taught that whoever eats what they earn by their own work, and gives some of it away, has found the path. The story goes that he chose a poor carpenter's plain bread over a rich man's feast.
neighbors.difference: Paul worked so the gospel would come free while he traveled and preached. For Sikhs, honest work is part of the spiritual life itself, joined with remembering God and sharing what you earn; nobody is asked to leave work behind.
neighbors.shared: the work of your hands can feed more than one table.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245 (paraphrase) · janamsakhi story of Bhai Lalo (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: what is hateful to you
neighbors.text: Today an early handbook said: whatever you wouldn't want done to you, don't do to another. A Jewish teacher said it in nearly those words. When a man asked Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot, Hillel answered: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn it.
neighbors.difference: The Didache sets the line on a path of following Jesus, beside the Lord's Prayer three times a day. For Hillel it sums up the Torah itself, and "go and learn" sends the asker into a lifetime of study and commandments.
neighbors.shared: start by not doing to anyone what would hurt you.

neighbors.heading: one road, another road
neighbors.text: Today the Didache opened with a choice: two ways, one of life and one of death. Buddhists know that fork too. The Dhammapada says one road leads to wealth and another to nirvana, and whoever sees the difference stops chasing honor. And it sums up the teaching plainly: do no evil, do good, and purify your own mind.
neighbors.difference: In the Didache, the way of life is love of God and neighbor, kept steady by daily prayer. In Buddhism, the good road leads toward nirvana, freedom from craving and suffering, walked by one's own effort.
neighbors.shared: every day, the road toward life can be chosen again.

neighbors.heading: a stranger, a traveler
neighbors.text: Today an old letter said Christians live in their own countries as sojourners. Muslims carry a saying with the same shape. The Prophet Muhammad took a companion by the shoulder and told him: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through. The companion, Ibn Umar, added: in the evening, don't wait for morning.
neighbors.difference: The letter to Diognetus also calls Christians the soul of the world, holding their cities together from within. The hadith turns the image toward readiness: a traveler goes light, using each day well, because the road ends with God.
neighbors.shared: you can love where you live and still travel light.

neighbors.heading: citizen of the world
neighbors.text: Today a letter said every homeland is foreign to Christians, and every foreign land home. Philosophers tried a double belonging too. Asked where he came from, Diogenes the Cynic said: I am a citizen of the world. Marcus Aurelius, an emperor, wrote that as Antoninus his city was Rome, but as a human being, his city was the world.
neighbors.difference: For the letter, Christians are strangers on earth because their true home is with God. For the Stoics, every person already belongs to one human city, here and now, joined by the reason all people share.
neighbors.shared: the person next to you belongs to your city too.
neighbors.sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.63 (paraphrase) · Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.44 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: service with no name on it
neighbors.text: Today Nicholas threw gold through a window and begged the father to tell no one. Sikhs call that spirit nishkam seva, service without wanting anything back. The Sukhmani Sahib says that one who serves with no thought of reward reaches the Lord. In a gurdwara, you may never learn who cooked your meal or looked after your shoes.
neighbors.difference: Nicholas's secret giving follows Jesus's words about alms done in secret, seen by the Father. For Sikhs, seva is also a discipline for the self: serving with your hands, side by side, wears down haumai, the ego.
neighbors.shared: the kindest gifts often arrive without a name.

neighbors.heading: a gift given rightly
neighbors.text: Today a bishop helped a family in the dark and wanted nothing back. The Bhagavad Gita describes that kind of gift. Krishna says the purest giving is given simply because giving is right, to someone who can't repay you, at the right place and time. A gift given grudgingly, or to get something back, it calls a lesser kind.
neighbors.difference: Nicholas's secrecy follows Jesus's words, so that only the Father sees. The Gita looks at the giver's inner state: the same act can be pure, restless or dark, depending on why, when and how it is given.
neighbors.shared: give because it's right, and then let the gift go.

neighbors.heading: whoever would tend me
neighbors.text: Today Pachomius learned that living together is harder than living alone, and that caring for the sick is part of it. Buddhist monks learned it too. Finding a monk lying sick and untended, the Buddha and Ananda washed him with their own hands. Then the Buddha told the community: whoever would tend me should tend the sick.
neighbors.difference: Pachomius' monks shared work, prayer and bread for the sake of Christ. The Buddhist sangha shares the path to awakening; its monks live on alms, and the community itself is one of the three refuges.
neighbors.shared: a real community notices when you're sick.

neighbors.heading: bear with one another
neighbors.text: Today Pachomius served monks who treated him like the help. Catholic religious life still knows that daily rub. The Rule of Benedict asks monks to bear with one another's weaknesses, of body or of character, with the greatest patience, and to try to be first in honoring each other. Catholic orders still live by rules like it: shared prayer, shared table.
neighbors.difference: Pachomius' Koinonia was an early experiment in living together. For Catholics, vowed community life is a lasting calling in the Church: men and women promise poverty, chastity and obedience, and share a common life.
neighbors.shared: patience with each other is how a home holds together.
neighbors.sources: Rule of Saint Benedict 72 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 915 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: meeting your shadow
neighbors.text: Today Augustine remembered stealing pears he didn't even want, and kept asking why. Psychologists ask that question too. Carl Jung called it the shadow: the parts of ourselves we'd rather not see. Everyone carries one, he wrote, and the less we admit it, the darker and denser it grows. Looking at it honestly is where change starts.
neighbors.difference: Augustine names his wrong in prayer, to a God he believes forgave him. Jung treats the shadow as part of the psyche to be known and integrated, not a sin to confess, work that can be done with or without faith.
neighbors.shared: the honest look at yourself is the brave one.

neighbors.heading: the inclination to do wrong
neighbors.text: Today Augustine looked hard at a boyhood wrong done just because it wasn't allowed. Jewish tradition names that pull: the yetzer hara, the inclination to do wrong, beside the yetzer tov, the inclination to do good. And the rabbis made a surprising claim. Without the yetzer hara, they said, no one would build a house, marry, or have children.
neighbors.difference: Augustine came to see the human will as bent, needing God's grace to heal it. The rabbis treat the yetzer hara as a drive God made, to be steered by Torah and good habits rather than a fallen nature.
neighbors.shared: everyone wrestles with a pull toward what they know is wrong.

neighbors.heading: first, hear
neighbors.text: Today Benedict's Rule began with one word: listen, with the ear of the heart. Hindu teaching starts with listening too. In an Upanishad, the sage Yajnavalkya tells his wife Maitreyi that the Self is to be seen, heard, reflected on, and meditated upon. Vedanta teachers make hearing, shravana, the first step. The oldest sacred texts are even called shruti: what was heard.
neighbors.difference: Benedict's listener attends to a teacher and to Christ's voice in scripture. In the Upanishad, what is heard points inward, to the Self, which Advaita teachers say is one with Brahman, the ultimate reality.
