Buddhists keep an old verse close: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." The Buddha also taught loving-kindness, metta, for all beings, and Buddhists still practice wishing it outward: to friends, to strangers, even to someone who has done harm.
neighbors.difference: The Amish forgive as they pray the Lord's Prayer, trusting God's forgiveness of them. In Buddhist teaching, letting go of hatred frees the heart that holds it; there's no divine forgiver, and actions still bear their fruit.
neighbors.shared: hatred doesn't heal hatred; something gentler has to.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 5 (Max Müller 1881) · Karaniya Metta Sutta (paraphrase) · Buddhaghosa, Visuddhimagga IX (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the visit to the cell
neighbors.text: Today forgiveness went to a family that hadn't asked for it. Catholics remember a scene like that. After Pope John Paul II was shot in St. Peter's Square, he went into the prison cell of the man who shot him, sat close, and talked with him quietly. He had already said he forgave him. Catholics pray: "forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors."
neighbors.difference: The Amish live forgiveness as a community habit, shaped by scripture and the Lord's Prayer. Catholics also receive God's forgiveness in the sacrament of reconciliation, where a priest speaks the words of absolution.
neighbors.shared: forgiveness can be chosen long before the day it's needed.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 6:12 (Douay-Rheims) · accounts of John Paul II's 1983 visit to Rebibbia prison (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a hand in the scanner
neighbors.text: Today a hand on a shoulder said: someone is with you. Psychologist James Coan tested that in a brain scanner. Married women waited for a mild shock alone, holding a stranger's hand, or holding their husband's. Holding a hand calmed the brain's threat response, and the husband's hand calmed it most, especially in the closest marriages.
neighbors.difference: In the Bible, the hand comes with prayer to God, and Christians trust God to act through it. The study measures what touch does in a body, and makes no claim about prayer either way.
neighbors.shared: being close enough to touch makes hard things lighter.

neighbors.heading: hands on a child's head
neighbors.text: Today hands carried a blessing. Many Jewish families do this every Friday night. At the Shabbat table, parents rest their hands on each child's head. For sons, the words come from Jacob blessing his grandsons: "God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." For daughters: as Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah. Then the priestly blessing: the Lord bless thee, and keep thee.
neighbors.difference: In the New Testament, hands often carry healing and the Holy Spirit, in Jesus' name. The Friday-night blessing passes on Jacob's words and the priests' blessing, parent to child, at home.
neighbors.shared: a hand and a blessing say: you are not alone.

neighbors.heading: a name, over and over
neighbors.text: Today a short line, sung again and again, began to sing the singer. Hindus call that japa: repeating a mantra or a name of God, often counted on a mala of beads. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that among offerings he is the offering of japa, repeating. Some Hindus say the same names every day for years, until the words go with them everywhere.
neighbors.difference: At Taizé the line is a prayer to God in Christ, often from scripture. Hindu japa repeats a mantra or one of God's names, such as Rama or Krishna, and many Hindus hold that the sacred sound itself carries power.
neighbors.shared: a few words repeated can carry you when thinking can't.

neighbors.heading: hearts find rest
neighbors.text: Today repetition became rest. Muslims call it dhikr, remembrance: short phrases said again and again, often counted on prayer beads or fingers. Subhan Allah, glory be to God. Alhamdulillah, praise be to God. Allahu akbar, God is greater. The Qur'an says: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!"
neighbors.difference: Taizé chants pray to God through Christ, in many languages, sung with harmony. Muslim dhikr remembers God alone, mostly in Arabic phrases the Prophet taught, said after prayer and through the day, often quietly.
neighbors.shared: the same few words, said with love, can quiet a busy heart.

neighbors.heading: every knee should bow
neighbors.text: Today the commandment guarded God's name. Catholics guard it with love. Paul's words, in the Douay-Rheims: "That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow." At Mass, Catholics are asked to bow their heads at the name of Jesus. And after Benediction they say the Divine Praises, "blessed be his holy name" among them, a prayer of praise and of amends for the Name misused.
neighbors.difference: Many Protestants share the commandment and the hallowing but not these devotions. Catholics add set gestures and prayers of honor and amends for the Name, like the Divine Praises, said before the Blessed Sacrament.
neighbors.shared: a name you love is a name you handle gently.
neighbors.sources: Philippians 2:10 (Douay-Rheims) · General Instruction of the Roman Missal 275 (paraphrase) · the Divine Praises (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: true is the name
neighbors.text: Today the commandment asked that God's name never be spent on nothing. Sikh scripture opens with the Name. The Mool Mantar, the first words of the Guru Granth Sahib, begins Ik Onkar, Sat Naam: one God, and the Name is truth. Sikhs practice Naam simran, remembering the Name again and again through the day, so it fills a life instead of slipping out empty.
neighbors.difference: The commandment mainly warns against misusing the Name, in oaths, curses or false causes. For Sikhs, the Name is the heart of devotion: repeated with love, all day long, it is how a person comes near God.
neighbors.shared: a name said with love never comes out empty.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Mool Mantar, Ang 1 · Japji Sahib (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the talebearer
neighbors.text: Today the commandment walked from the courtroom to the lunch table. Jewish teaching walks there too. The Torah says: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people." The rabbis called hurtful talk lashon hara, the evil tongue, and counted it harmful even when true. The Talmud says shaming someone in public is like shedding blood.
neighbors.difference: Christian teachers like Luther ground it in loving the neighbor, members of one body. Jewish law spells out the details, and one classic book, the Hafetz Hayyim, teaches exactly when speaking of others is allowed.
neighbors.shared: speak of people as if they were in the room.
neighbors.sources: Leviticus 19:16 (JPS 1917) · Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b (paraphrase) · Israel Meir Kagan, Hafetz Hayyim (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: right speech
neighbors.text: Today the commandment covered gossip, spin and half-truths. The Buddha put speech on his Eightfold Path. Right speech, he taught, means holding back from four things: false speech, divisive speech that splits friends apart, harsh speech, and idle chatter. Elsewhere he gives a test for good words: said at the right time, true, gentle, helpful, and with a kind heart.
neighbors.difference: In the commandment, a lie wrongs a neighbor before God. The Buddha weighs speech by its harm and its fruit for speaker and listener alike, without a God who commands it.
neighbors.shared: words can wound or heal, so choose them with care.

neighbors.heading: the real strong one
neighbors.text: Today the Bible said slow to anger, not never angry. Muslims hold a saying of the Prophet: the strong one is not the one who wins at wrestling, but the one who controls himself when angry. The Qur'an praises those "who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind." Another saying advises: if you're angry while standing, sit down.
neighbors.difference: Christian teaching draws the line where anger starts wanting someone hurt, and points to Jesus' grieving anger. Islam also honors anger at wrong for God's sake, and gives practical steps: seek refuge in God, sit, or lie down.
neighbors.shared: anger can come; it just doesn't get to drive.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Good Manners (paraphrase) · Qur'an 3:134 (Pickthall 1930) · Sunan Abu Dawud, Book of Etiquette (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the right anger
neighbors.text: Today Paul said: be angry, and sin not. Aristotle agreed that anger has a place. Anyone can get angry, he wrote; that's easy. But to be angry with the right person, to the right degree, at the right time, for the right reason and in the right way is not easy. He called the good middle gentleness. Seneca added a cure: delay.
neighbors.difference: Christian patience echoes God, slow to anger and plenteous in mercy, and leans on grace. Aristotle and Seneca build good temper by reason and practice, a human skill open to anyone, whatever they believe about God.
neighbors.shared: hear first, speak later, get angry last.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.9 and IV.5 (paraphrase) · Seneca, On Anger (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Works of mercy for the body

neighbors.heading: water for both sides
neighbors.text: Today the hungry stranger and Christ shared one face. Sikhs tell of Bhai Kanhaiya, who carried water through a battle at Anandpur, giving drink to wounded soldiers on both sides. When Sikhs complained, Guru Gobind Singh asked him why. He answered that he saw no enemy, only the Guru's face in every man. The Guru gave him ointment too.
neighbors.difference: In Matthew, Christ meets us in the least, and serving them is serving him. For Sikhs, the one Light shines in everyone, and seva, selfless service, is done for the Guru and God present in each person, without seeking reward.
neighbors.shared: the person in need is never a stranger to God.

neighbors.heading: the guest as God
neighbors.text: Today feeding a hungry person was feeding Christ. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher's parting words to his students say: let your mother be as a god to you, your father, your teacher, and your guest. Atithi devo bhava: the guest is God. Hindu homes traditionally serve the guest first, and some temples feed anyone who comes, free.
neighbors.difference: Jesus says the hungry are his brethren, and to serve them is to serve him. The Upanishad asks you to honor the guest as God, and many Hindus see the divine within every being.
neighbors.shared: whoever comes to your door deserves your best plate.

neighbors.heading: they fear as you do
neighbors.text: Today some Christians laid down the rifle. The first Buddhist precept is to refrain from taking life. The Dhammapada says: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." Monks and nuns keep it strictly, and Buddhist teachers have often spoken up for peace.
neighbors.difference: The peace churches refuse to fight because Jesus said resist not evil, and they trust God with the outcome. The Buddhist precept grows from seeing others' fear as your own, and from karma; it isn't a command from God.
neighbors.shared: the other person fears harm just as you do.

neighbors.heading: a soldier puts down his sword
neighbors.text: Today the peace churches said: not for us. Catholics remember Martin of Tours, a Roman soldier who became a Christian. His early biographer says that before a battle he told the emperor: I am a soldier of Christ; it is not lawful for me to fight. He offered to stand in the front line unarmed. Catholics honor him as a saint.
neighbors.difference: Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren have long taught nonviolence as their church's way. Catholic teaching keeps the just war tradition, yet praises those who renounce violence and asks that conscientious objectors be treated fairly.
neighbors.shared: peace can take more courage than a fight.
neighbors.sources: Sulpicius Severus, Life of Saint Martin 4 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2306, 2311 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: made to work together
neighbors.text: Today one blood meant one family. Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor and Stoic, began his mornings ready to meet rude and unkind people, and reminded himself: they are my kin, sharing the same reason I do. We are made to work together, he wrote, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the upper and lower rows of teeth. To work against each other is against nature.
neighbors.difference: Paul grounds human kinship in God the maker, and in the image of God in every face. Marcus grounds it in the reason every person shares; his Stoic god is the reason running through the whole world.
neighbors.shared: the stranger across the room is family you haven't met.

neighbors.heading: one ancestor for everyone
neighbors.text: Today Paul said every nation was made of one blood. The Mishnah asks why God began with a single human. So that no one could say to another, my father was greater than yours, it answers, and to teach that each person is a whole world. A king stamps coins from one die and they all look alike; God stamped everyone from Adam, and no two are the same.
neighbors.difference: Paul sets one blood beside a new oneness in Christ. The Mishnah grounds human equality in Adam, while the covenant at Sinai gives the Jewish people their own particular calling.
neighbors.shared: no one gets to say their ancestors were greater.

neighbors.heading: no hate for any being
neighbors.text: Today the Bible asked for one concrete good done for an enemy. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes the devotee he loves: one who hates no being, friendly and compassionate, the same to friend and foe, in honor and in insult. Gandhi, who treasured the Gita, put it to work: he set out to resist wrongs while bearing no hatred toward the wrongdoer.
neighbors.difference: Jesus asks his followers to love enemies as the Father does, who sends rain on the just and the unjust. The Gita roots it in seeing the same Self in every being, and a steady mind beyond friend and foe.
neighbors.shared: you can refuse to hate and still stand against a wrong.

neighbors.heading: repel it with something better
neighbors.text: Today the Torah sent an enemy's ox home. The Qur'an asks for the same turn: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend." Muslims remember the Prophet entering Mecca, the city that had driven him out, and pardoning many who had fought him.
neighbors.difference: Jesus asks his followers to love enemies and pray for them, even under persecution. The Qur'an also allows a wrong to be answered with equal justice, while calling forgiveness and patience the greater way.
neighbors.shared: one good deed can turn an enemy toward a friend.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 41:34 (Pickthall 1930) · Qur'an 42:40 (paraphrase) · accounts of the conquest of Mecca in the sira (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the meal called thanks
neighbors.text: Today Jesus gave thanks on the night he was betrayed. Catholics named their central worship for it. The Catechism explains that Eucharist comes from a Greek word for thanksgiving, and calls the Mass a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the Father. Its prayers say it is right to give God thanks always and everywhere, and the people answer at the end: thanks be to God.
neighbors.difference: Paul asks every Christian to give thanks in everything, in prayer and grace at meals. Catholics also gather that thanks into the Mass itself, where they believe Christ is truly present and offered to the Father.
neighbors.shared: thanks can be said even on the hardest night.

neighbors.heading: your will is sweet
neighbors.text: Today Paul asked people in grief to give thanks in everything. Sikhs sing a line of Guru Arjan's: whatever you do tastes sweet to me. Sikhs remember that he met a cruel death in Lahore calmly, accepting God's will. And every Ardas, the Sikh prayer, closes: by your will, may all be well, sarbat da bhala.
neighbors.difference: Paul's thanks rests on God's will in Christ Jesus. Sikhs speak of hukam, God's order running through all things, and bhana, accepting it as sweet, with chardi kala, rising spirits, even in hardship.
neighbors.shared: gratitude doesn't wait for the trouble to pass.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Asa, Guru Arjan (paraphrase) · Ardas (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a blessing for bad news too
neighbors.text: Today Fortune's wheel turned Boethius from high to low. Jewish law meets that turn with a blessing. The Mishnah says a person must bless God for the bad just as for the good. Hearing good news, Jews say: blessed is He who is good and does good. Hearing of a death: blessed is the true Judge. Ecclesiastes says: "God hath made even the one as well as the other."
neighbors.difference: Boethius finds comfort through reasoning, as Philosophy leads him to God, the still center. The Jewish blessings don't explain the loss; they meet it with a set sentence, said in the moment, naming God as judge.
neighbors.shared: a hard day can still be met with a blessing.

neighbors.heading: eight winds
neighbors.text: Today Fortune's wheel kept turning. The Buddha named what turns it: eight worldly conditions. Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. They come to everyone, he said, the wise and the unwise alike. The difference is how they're met: the one who sees that they pass isn't carried off by gain or crushed by loss.
neighbors.difference: Philosophy leads Boethius past Fortune to God, the highest good at the still center. The Buddha points to seeing the conditions as passing and not-self, and to freedom in letting go, not to a God at the center.
neighbors.shared: what can be taken away was only on loan.

neighbors.heading: signs for people who think
neighbors.text: Today Aquinas walked from a moving world back to a first mover. Muslims walk that road too. The Qur'an keeps pointing at the world itself: the heavens and the earth, night following day, are signs for people who think. Muslim thinkers like al-Ghazali argued that whatever begins to exist has a cause, and the chain leads back to God, who has no beginning.
neighbors.difference: Aquinas's ways reach a first cause, and the Bible then names this God Father, Son and Holy Spirit. For Muslims, the signs point to the one God, who, the Qur'an teaches, is utterly one and unlike anything he made.
neighbors.shared: the world itself can turn your eyes toward where it came from.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 3:190 (paraphrase) · al-Ghazali, Moderation in Belief (al-Iqtisad fi al-I'tiqad), on the cause of what begins (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the philosopher's first mover
neighbors.text: Aquinas didn't start this road alone. He called Aristotle simply "the Philosopher," and the five ways lean on him. Aristotle watched a world full of change and reasoned that the chain of movers can't run back forever. There must be a first mover, itself unmoved, that moves everything else, he said, the way something loved moves the one who loves it.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle reached his first mover by reason alone, with no scripture and no prayer. His unmoved mover doesn't create the world from nothing or care for it; Aquinas's God does both, and is the God Christians pray to.
neighbors.shared: a curious mind, asking why, is already walking toward something.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Physics VIII; Metaphysics XII.7 (paraphrase) · Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 3

neighbors.heading: you are my mother
neighbors.text: Today Julian called God our Mother as truly as our Father. The Sikh Gurus sang those two words side by side. In a hymn of Guru Arjan in the Guru Granth Sahib, the singer says to God: you are my father, you are my mother, you are my kin and my brother. You protect me everywhere, so why should I be afraid?
neighbors.difference: Julian gives motherhood above all to Jesus, God made flesh. For Sikhs, God is one and formless, never born, so father and mother are ways to name a closeness, not a person who took a body.
neighbors.shared: the love that made you is tender as a mother's.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 103 (Guru Arjan, Raag Majh) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: mother of this world
neighbors.text: Hindus have long called God mother. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says he is the father of this world and its mother too, the one who holds it up. And Hindus pray to God as the Goddess, Devi. One old hymn praises the goddess who lives in every being in the form of a mother, again and again: we bow to her.
neighbors.difference: Julian keeps "Father" and calls God "Mother" just as truly, above all in Christ, within one God in three persons. Many Hindus also worship the Goddess as God herself, with her own temples, festivals and names.
neighbors.shared: you can call to God the way a child calls home.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 9.17 (paraphrase) · Devi Mahatmya, ch. 5 ("ya devi sarvabhuteshu matrirupena samsthita") (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: meeting in harmony
neighbors.text: Today Khomiakov pictured a church that is many and one, freely, in love. The Buddha cared about that too. Near the end of his life, he told his monks their community would thrive as long as they met often, met in harmony, rose in harmony, and did their work in harmony. The sangha, the community, is one of the three jewels Buddhists take refuge in.
neighbors.difference: For Khomiakov, the church's unity is one life shared in Christ, held by the Spirit's love. The sangha's harmony serves the path to awakening; Buddhists don't speak of it as one body with a divine head.
neighbors.shared: being many and one takes freedom, patience and showing up together.

neighbors.heading: one, and catholic
neighbors.text: Catholics say today's word in the creed: one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church. Their Bible names the ties: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism," and above all charity, "the bond of perfection." The Catechism calls the Church's unity a gift from God that grows. And like the apostles in Acts, Catholic bishops meet in councils to decide together.
neighbors.difference: Khomiakov saw unity kept by the whole church together, with no single head on earth. Catholics see that unity also served by the pope, the bishop of Rome, whom the Catechism calls a visible source and foundation of unity.
neighbors.shared: love is the thread that keeps many people one.
neighbors.sources: Ephesians 4:5; Colossians 3:14 (Douay-Rheims) · Nicene Creed · Catechism of the Catholic Church 813–820, 882 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: what you attend to
neighbors.text: Today Weil called attention, at its highest, prayer. A psychologist reached a nearby place by another road. William James wrote: "My experience is what I agree to attend to. Only those items which I notice shape my mind." What you look at, again and again, becomes the shape of your life. And a friend who really listens helps shape theirs.
neighbors.difference: For Weil, attention opens the soul to God, and even geometry homework can be practice for prayer. James describes attention as how any mind is built, believer or not, and leaves the question of God to other pages.
neighbors.shared: where you put your attention, you put your love.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. 11, "Attention"

neighbors.heading: kavanah, the heart aimed
neighbors.text: Jews have a word for today's idea: kavanah, directing the heart. The Mishnah remembers the pious ones of old, who would wait an hour before they prayed, just to turn their hearts toward their Father in heaven. Maimonides taught that prayer without kavanah isn't really prayer. The words need a person behind them.
neighbors.difference: Weil found the highest attention could be prayer in itself, even over a math problem. Jewish prayer keeps fixed words and fixed times, keva, and asks for kavanah inside them, so set words and a turned heart go together.
neighbors.shared: a prayer is only as present as the person saying it.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah Berakhot 5:1 (paraphrase) · Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Prayer 4:15 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: do it as an offering
neighbors.text: Today Rahner found God in the kitchen and the commute. The Bhagavad Gita says something close. Krishna tells Arjuna: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give away, whatever effort you make, do it as an offering to me. Some Hindu families live that out by offering food to God before they eat it, so even lunch becomes worship.
neighbors.difference: Rahner speaks of meeting the Spirit, often without feeling it, in ordinary faithfulness. In the Gita, the offering goes to Krishna, whom Hindus worship as God, and acting without grasping at results is part of the path to freedom.
neighbors.shared: an ordinary day can be holy ground, done with care.

neighbors.heading: as though you see him
neighbors.text: Muslims have a word for worship that fills the whole day: ihsan. In a well-known hadith, the angel Jibril asks the Prophet what it is. He answers: to worship God as though you see him, and if you don't see him, he sees you. With that in mind, washing before prayer, working honestly and a kind word at home can all be worship.
neighbors.difference: Rahner's mysticism often feels like nothing at all, a quiet yes in an ordinary task. Islam also builds the day around five set prayers, so the remembrance of God comes back at fixed hours, wherever you are.
neighbors.shared: God isn't only found far away; maybe right where you're standing.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 50; Sahih Muslim 8 (the hadith of Jibril) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: carved into the candle
neighbors.text: Catholics hold today's words in their hands. At the Easter Vigil, the priest may cut a cross into the great Paschal candle and trace the Greek letters alpha and omega, praying: Christ yesterday and today, the beginning and the end, Alpha and Omega. All time belongs to him. That candle then stands beside baptisms and funerals, the beginnings and endings of a life.
neighbors.difference: Both read the same Revelation. The difference is in the hands: Catholics carry the verse into a rite, marking it in wax with the year's numbers, while many Protestant churches keep it in reading, preaching and song.
neighbors.shared: the one who was there at the start will be there at the end.
neighbors.sources: Revelation 1:8 · Roman Missal, Easter Vigil, preparation of the Paschal candle (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: true in the beginning
neighbors.text: Today God signed the letter: who is, who was, who is to come. Sikhs open their scripture with words close to that. Right after the Mul Mantar, at the start of Guru Nanak's Japji, the one God is called true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and, says Nanak, true forever. Many Sikhs recite it each morning.
neighbors.difference: Christians hear these words fulfilled in Jesus, God come in the flesh. The Mul Mantar calls the timeless one ajooni, beyond birth, so Sikhs don't speak of God taking a body; the Guru is the one who reveals.
neighbors.shared: before every beginning and after every ending, something true remains.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Mul Mantar and the opening salok of Japji) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: wake up, sleepers
neighbors.text: Today a church slept inside its good name and heard: be watchful. Jews hear a wake-up call every autumn. On Rosh Hashanah the shofar, a ram's horn, sounds. Maimonides wrote what it says without words: wake up, you sleepers, from your sleep; search your deeds and return. Then come the days of looking honestly at the year.
neighbors.difference: Revelation's call comes from the risen Christ to one church, with his coming in view. The shofar sounds each year in the Jewish calendar, and return, teshuvah, means turning back to God and to the people you've wronged.
neighbors.shared: it's never too late to wake up and begin again.
neighbors.sources: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 3:4 (paraphrase) · Leviticus 23:24

neighbors.heading: the one who woke up
neighbors.text: Buddhists build a whole path on today's words. Buddha means the awakened one. A sutta tells of a man who asked him: are you a god? No, he said. Remember me as awake. The Dhammapada puts it plainly: "Earnestness is the path of immortality," and thoughtlessness the path of death. Wake up, and stay awake.
neighbors.difference: Sardis wakes up to Christ, who calls and comes. In Buddhist teaching, waking up means seeing clearly how things are, and no god does it for you: the Buddha shows the way, and each person walks it.
neighbors.shared: a sleepy life can still be woken, gently, starting today.
neighbors.sources: Dona Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 4.36 (paraphrase) · Dhammapada 21 (Max Müller 1881)

neighbors.heading: that you may know one another
neighbors.text: Today heaven held every nation and tongue, and none were melted into one. The Qur'an says something close about this world: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." The differences are there so we'd meet. And at Hajj, pilgrims from every land stand together, dressed alike and simply.
neighbors.difference: Revelation's crowd stands before the throne and the Lamb, made clean by his death. The same Qur'an verse goes on to say the noblest in God's sight is the one best in conduct, and each pilgrim stands before God alone.
neighbors.shared: every language and face was meant to be met, not erased.

neighbors.heading: a citizen of the world
neighbors.text: Philosophers dreamed of today's crowd too. Asked where he came from, Diogenes is remembered for answering: I am a citizen of the world. Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor, wrote in his notebook that as Antoninus his city was Rome, but as a human being, his city was the world. The person across any border is a fellow citizen.
neighbors.difference: Revelation gathers the nations around God and the Lamb, with every tear wiped away. These philosophers found their world-city in shared human reason, here and now, and made no promise about tears or what comes after.
neighbors.shared: no border is wide enough to make a stranger less human.
neighbors.sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers VI.63 (paraphrase) · Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.44 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the soul as bride
neighbors.text: Today the Bible arrives at a wedding. A Sikh wedding is a hymn about God. In the Anand Karaj, the couple walk four times around the Guru Granth Sahib while the Laavan of Guru Ram Das are sung. Each round tells of the soul drawing closer to God, and the last sings of joyful union with the Beloved.
neighbors.difference: In Revelation, the bride is the whole people of God, married to Christ, the Lamb. In Sikh teaching, every soul is a bride longing for the one formless Lord, and a married couple walk that path together.
neighbors.shared: love between two people can be a picture of love for God.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 773–774 (the Laavan, Guru Ram Das, Raag Suhi) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: mine is the mountain-lifter
neighbors.text: Hindu devotion knows this bride. The poet-saint Mirabai, tradition says, gave her heart to Krishna as a girl and called him her husband all her life. One of her songs begins: mine is Giridhar Gopal, the cowherd who lifted the mountain, and no other. People still sing it, a soul's love for God in a bride's words.
neighbors.difference: Revelation's bride is the church, many people made one and married to the Lamb. Mirabai's love is personal and fierce, one soul and Krishna, whom she worshipped as God, sung even when, tradition says, her family disapproved.
neighbors.shared: the deepest longing can sound like a love song.

neighbors.heading: a medicine for suffering
neighbors.text: Today a tree's leaves heal the nations. Buddhists remember a tree too: the Buddha awoke beneath one, the Bodhi tree. And his teaching is often pictured as medicine. The four noble truths go like a doctor's visit: there is suffering; it has a cause; it can end; here is the path. Some Buddhists also pray to the Medicine Buddha for healing.
neighbors.difference: Revelation's healing flows from the throne of God and the Lamb, in a city made new. In Buddhist teaching, the cure is a path each person walks, seeing clearly and letting go of craving; the Buddha is the doctor, not a creator.
neighbors.shared: every wound, even between peoples, can begin to mend.
neighbors.sources: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11 (paraphrase) · the Medicine Buddha (Bhaisajyaguru) Sutra (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: physician of souls and bodies
neighbors.text: Catholics read today's leaves alongside Ezekiel's trees, with fruit for food and leaves for medicine. The Catechism calls Jesus "physician of our souls and bodies," and names two sacraments of healing: confession, for the soul's wounds, and the anointing of the sick, with oil and prayer. The healing Revelation pictures, Catholics believe, has already begun.
neighbors.difference: Christians share the verse. The difference is in practice: Catholics count confession and anointing among seven sacraments, while many Protestant churches pray for the sick and confess sin without calling these sacraments.
neighbors.shared: healing begins with someone close enough to touch the wound.
neighbors.sources: Ezekiel 47:12 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1421 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: you could leave life now
neighbors.text: Philosophers kept today's skull on the desk too. Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome, wrote to himself that he might leave life this very moment, so every act and thought should be shaped by that. Not to make himself gloomy. To stop wasting days on anger and other people's opinions. Remembering the end was his way of waking up to now.
neighbors.difference: The psalm asks God to teach the counting, and Christians hold a hope beyond the grave. Marcus left that question open: if there are gods, nothing to fear; if not, still live well today.
neighbors.shared: knowing the days are few can make each one count.

neighbors.heading: one day before you die
neighbors.text: Psalm 90 is Jewish scripture too, titled a prayer of Moses. The rabbis made its lesson practical. Rabbi Eliezer taught: repent one day before your death. His students asked, but who knows the day they'll die? Exactly, he said. So repent today, in case you die tomorrow, and all your days will be spent returning.
neighbors.difference: Christians number their days with Christ's death and rising in view, and some with Lent's ashes. Jews hear it at the High Holy Days, when a prayer asks who will live and who will die, and says repentance, prayer and charity soften the decree.
neighbors.shared: today is a good day to set things right.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah Avot 2:10; Talmud, Shabbat 153a (paraphrase) · Unetaneh Tokef (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: water for the ancestors
neighbors.text: Hindu families keep today's prayer too. In shraddha rites, a son or relative offers rice balls, pinda, and water for those who have died, saying their names, often for three generations back. Each year, in the fortnight called Pitru Paksha, families remember their ancestors with food and prayer. Love keeps feeding the ones you can no longer see.
neighbors.difference: Christians who pray for the dead ask God's mercy and rest for a soul. Hindu rites are offered to help the departed on their way and to honor the ancestors, within a belief in rebirth that Christians don't share.
neighbors.shared: the people we've lost are still worth remembering out loud.
neighbors.sources: Manusmriti, ch. 3 (the shraddha rites) (paraphrase) · Bhagavad Gita 1.42 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a child who prays
neighbors.text: Muslims pray for the dead from the first day. The funeral prayer, salat al-janazah, is said standing, asking God's forgiveness and mercy for the one who has died. And the Prophet said that when a person dies, their deeds end, except for three: charity that keeps giving, knowledge that helps others, and a righteous child who prays for them.
neighbors.difference: In Christian prayer, rest and light for the dead come through Christ's death and rising. Muslims ask God directly for mercy, and the hadith adds that a person's good keeps flowing after death through what they left behind.
neighbors.shared: love doesn't stop speaking when the one we love is gone.

neighbors.heading: what name do you give?
neighbors.text: The Catholic rite begins with a question to the parents: what name do you give your child? Later the priest says that name over the water: I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The Catechism puts it simply: God calls each one by name, and everyone's name is sacred.
neighbors.difference: Many Protestant churches baptize with the same water and words. Catholics count baptism first of seven sacraments, and the Church encourages a saint's name, so a patron walks beside the child.
neighbors.shared: a name said out loud with love says: you belong here.
neighbors.sources: Isaiah 43:1 · Rite of Baptism for Children (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2156–2158, 2165 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a name from the page
neighbors.text: Sikh families give a name with their scripture open. In the naming ceremony, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened for a hukam, the Guru's word for that moment, and the first letter of that hymn guides the child's name. The name is announced to the gathering, with Singh for a boy or Kaur for a girl, and a sweet offering, karah prashad, is shared.
neighbors.difference: In baptism, water joins a person to Christ's death and rising. A Sikh naming isn't an initiation: that comes later, with Amrit, when a person chooses to take the Khalsa vows for themselves.
neighbors.shared: every child's name can come wrapped in a blessing.
neighbors.sources: Sikh Rehat Maryada, the naming ceremony (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: silence is praise
neighbors.text: Jewish tradition knows today's waiting too. In the Mishnah, Rabban Shimon, son of Rabban Gamliel, says he grew up all his days among the sages and found nothing better for a person than silence. Maimonides, writing that no words can hold God, read a psalm's line as: to you, silence is praise. And Elijah's still small voice is Jewish scripture first.
neighbors.difference: Quaker silence is the whole service, waiting for anyone to be moved to speak. Jewish prayer is mostly words, said together at set times; silence lives inside it, as in the Amidah, prayed standing with lips moving, barely heard.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the truest thing in a room is the quiet.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah Avot 1:17 (paraphrase) · Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed I.59, on Psalm 65:2 (paraphrase) · 1 Kings 19:12

neighbors.heading: noble silence
neighbors.text: The Buddha gave his monks two choices when they gathered: talk about the teaching, or keep noble silence. Buddhist retreats often keep it for days: no chatting, eyes down, just sitting and walking in quiet. In some Zen halls, people sit facing a wall, not to shut anyone out, but to see their own mind clearly.
neighbors.difference: Friends wait in silence for God's voice, and anyone may stand to speak. Buddhist silence isn't waiting for a message from God; it's a way to watch thoughts rise and fall until the mind settles and sees.
neighbors.shared: quiet, kept together, can hold a whole room of people.

neighbors.heading: love and mercy
neighbors.text: Today two people promised, for better, for worse. The Qur'an names marriage among God's signs: spouses made from one another, so they can find rest in each other, with love and mercy placed between them. At a Muslim wedding, the nikah, both agree before witnesses, and the groom gives the bride a gift, the mahr, that is hers alone.
neighbors.difference: A Christian wedding vow is made before God, "till death us do part," and many churches call marriage a sacrament or a covenant. In Islam, nikah is a solemn contract blessed by God, and divorce is allowed as a last resort.
neighbors.shared: a good marriage is a place where two people can rest.

neighbors.heading: spaces in your togetherness
neighbors.text: Kahlil Gibran's The Prophet is often read at weddings. On marriage he writes: "But let there be spaces in your togetherness, And let the winds of the heavens dance between you." Love one another, he says, but don't make love a chain. Stand together, like the pillars of a temple, which stand apart.
neighbors.difference: The prayer book's vow binds two lives into one flesh before God. Gibran keeps two selves distinct inside the love, and his poem asks no one to name a God; couples of any belief can say it.
neighbors.shared: love grows best when both people still have room to breathe.

neighbors.heading: the pool of the Guru
neighbors.text: Today water waited at the church door. Sikhs know that walk. At the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the Golden Temple stands in a pool, and pilgrims bathe in it. Guru Arjan sang that bathing in Guru Ram Das's pool washes away the wrongs you've done. At any gurdwara, visitors take off their shoes and cover their heads before going in.
neighbors.difference: Baptism's water joins a person to Christ once, for good. For Sikhs, outer washing is respect and cleanliness; Guru Nanak taught that the true bath is inward, at the shrine within, remembering God's Name.
neighbors.shared: you can walk in carrying the dust and leave washed.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 625 (Guru Arjan, Raag Sorath) (paraphrase) · Japji, pauri 21, Ang 4 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: water before worship
neighbors.text: Hindus often meet God after water too. Many temples have a tank beside them, and worshippers wash hands and feet, or bathe, before going in. At home, a puja often begins by sprinkling water to purify. And an old Vedic hymn calls to the waters like loving mothers, asking them to make us clean and strong.
neighbors.difference: Christians are baptized once, entering by water into Christ's death and rising. Hindu washing is done again and again, before puja and in sacred rivers like the Ganga, to make body and mind ready for God.
neighbors.shared: a little water can help a heart arrive.
neighbors.sources: Rig Veda 10.9 (the hymn to the waters) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a fragrance against the wind
neighbors.text: Buddhists light incense at shrines too, often three sticks, and watch it burn down: a quiet lesson that everything passes. The Dhammapada adds a twist. The scent of flowers, even sandalwood, can't travel against the wind, it says. But the fragrance of good people does. It spreads in every direction.
neighbors.difference: In the Bible, the smoke rises with prayer toward God, who hears. A Buddhist incense offering honors the Buddha and reminds the one offering of impermanence and goodness; it isn't sent up to a creator God.
neighbors.shared: goodness carries further than any smoke can rise.

neighbors.heading: reverence and prayer
neighbors.text: At a solemn Catholic Mass, a censer swings over the altar, the Gospel book, the bread and wine, and then the people themselves. The Mass instructions explain it: incense expresses reverence and prayer. At evening prayer, Catholics sing the psalm: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight."
neighbors.difference: Christians share the psalm. Many Protestant churches keep it as words, with no smoke in worship; the Catholic Church, like the Orthodox, keeps incense rising in the liturgy itself.
neighbors.shared: prayer doesn't stay on the ground; it rises.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 140:2 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 141:2 in many Bibles) · General Instruction of the Roman Missal 276 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a review before sleep
neighbors.text: Philosophers had a bedtime practice too. Seneca wrote that each night, once the lamp was out and the house was quiet, he went over his whole day, what he'd said and done, hiding nothing from himself. And then, he said, how sweet the sleep that followed. Not fear of judgment. A gentle accounting, so tomorrow could be a little better.
neighbors.difference: The child's prayer hands the night to God's keeping. Seneca's review hands the day to his own honest look; he is his own judge, fair and gentle, and needs no one else watching.
neighbors.shared: it's a kindness to let the day go before sleep.

neighbors.heading: into his hand
neighbors.text: Jews say a bedtime Shema too: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Before it comes a blessing to the One who brings sleep to the eyes. And the hymn Adon Olam ends: into his hand I place my spirit, when I sleep and when I wake; the LORD is with me, I will not fear.
neighbors.difference: Christians often pray at night through Jesus, who on the cross prayed the psalm's words, into thy hands. Jewish bedtime prayer goes to God directly, with the Shema at its center, said morning and night.
neighbors.shared: you can let go of the day; someone is keeping watch.
neighbors.sources: Deuteronomy 6:4 (JPS 1917) · Talmud, Berakhot 60b (the bedtime blessing) (paraphrase) · Adon Olam (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: walking to Pandharpur
neighbors.text: Hindus walk too. Every year in Maharashtra, pilgrims called Warkaris walk for weeks to the temple of Vitthal at Pandharpur. They carry the sandals of saints in palanquins and sing the songs of Tukaram and Dnyaneshwar all the way. Strangers become family on the road, and the walking itself is worship.
neighbors.difference: On the Camino, the road leads to an apostle's tomb, and some walkers hear Jesus's "I am the way." The Warkaris walk to see Vitthal, a form of Krishna whom they worship as God, singing his name the whole way.
neighbors.shared: a long road, walked together, can turn strangers into family.
neighbors.sources: the Pandharpur Wari (living tradition) · the abhangs of Tukaram (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: here I am
neighbors.text: Muslims have a pilgrimage at the center of the faith: Hajj to Mecca. The Qur'an calls it a duty to God for everyone able to make the journey. Pilgrims set aside their usual clothes for simple ones, so king and farmer look alike, and retrace steps remembered from Abraham and Hagar, calling out: here I am, O God, here I am.
neighbors.difference: The Camino is a free choice, walked for prayer, grief or wonder, and no Christian has to go. Hajj is one of Islam's five pillars, owed once in a lifetime by those who are able, at a set time each year.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the heart finds its way once the feet start moving.

neighbors.heading: the works of mercy
neighbors.text: Catholics turn today's gut-deep word into a list you can do. Jesus says: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in." From that, the Church names works of mercy: feed, give drink, clothe, shelter, visit the sick and prisoners, bury the dead.
neighbors.difference: Christians share Matthew 25. Catholic teaching gathers it into a set list, works of mercy for the body and for the soul, from feeding the hungry to comforting the sorrowful and praying for the living and the dead.
neighbors.shared: compassion isn't finished until it reaches someone's hands.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 25:35 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the bull of compassion
neighbors.text: Guru Nanak gave compassion a big job. In the Japji, he asks what holds up the earth, since old stories said a bull carried it. His answer: the bull is dharma, righteousness, and dharma is the child of compassion. Sikhs put that into hands and feet in the langar, the free kitchen where anyone, of any faith, sits and eats together.
neighbors.difference: In the Gospels, compassion flows from Jesus, and Christians see God's own heart in him. Sikhs see compassion as the root of righteousness, lived out in seva, selfless service, as a way of remembering the one God.
neighbors.shared: the world stays standing on small acts of kindness.

neighbors.heading: a guide for the perplexed
neighbors.text: Jewish thinkers flew on both wings too. Saadia Gaon wrote that reason and revelation reach the same truth, and that God gave the Torah so people wouldn't have to wait a lifetime to arrive. Maimonides wrote his Guide for the Perplexed for a student torn between philosophy and scripture, to show him he didn't have to tear himself in two.
neighbors.difference: John Paul II's two wings lift the spirit toward truth, fully shown in Christ. Jewish thinkers keep Torah and its commandments at the center, and reason inside a long, open argument, the Talmud, where good questions are prized.
neighbors.shared: an honest question can be part of a faithful life.
neighbors.sources: Saadia Gaon, The Book of Beliefs and Opinions, introduction (paraphrase) · Maimonides, The Guide for the Perplexed, introduction (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: test it yourself
neighbors.text: The Buddha once met villagers, the Kalamas, confused by teachers who each said only they were right. He told them not to accept a teaching just because of tradition, scripture, logic or a teacher's fame. Test it yourselves, he said: when you know a thing leads to harm and suffering, give it up; when it leads to welfare and happiness, take it up.
neighbors.difference: Christians hold reason and faith as two gifts from one God, with revelation trusted beyond what reason can reach. The Buddha asks for tested experience, points to no creator, and says even a revered teacher's word should be checked.
neighbors.shared: your questions are welcome on the way.

neighbors.heading: trust, and tie your camel
neighbors.text: Muslims have a word for today's throw: tawakkul, trust in God. The Qur'an promises that whoever puts their trust in God, he will be enough for them. But trust isn't sitting still. A hadith tells of a man who asked the Prophet whether to tie his camel or trust God. Tie it, the Prophet said, and trust.
neighbors.difference: Peter ties casting care to God's care, shown in Christ. Muslims place their trust in God alongside honest effort, and in hard moments many say hasbunallah: God is enough for us.
neighbors.shared: do what you can, then let the rest be held.

neighbors.heading: what's yours to carry
neighbors.text: Philosophers drew today's line too. Epictetus opens his handbook by sorting: some things are in our power, and some are not. Our own judgments, choices and efforts are ours. Other people's opinions, our health, how things turn out are not. Peace, he says, comes from carrying what's yours and setting down the rest.
neighbors.difference: Peter asks you to throw worry onto God, who cares for you. Epictetus sorts the worry first, what's in your power and what isn't; his calm comes from training your own judgments, where he says freedom lives.
neighbors.shared: you were never built to carry everything.

neighbors.heading: frighten no one
neighbors.text: Sikh teaching holds both halves of today's question. Guru Tegh Bahadur wrote that the wise one frightens no one and is afraid of no one. And Guru Gobind Singh, in a letter to the emperor Aurangzeb, wrote that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Never first. Only to protect.
neighbors.difference: Christians differ: some refuse all weapons, following Jesus's words on enemies; others hold the just war tradition. Sikhs honor the saint-soldier, ready to defend the weak, and keep the kirpan as a reminder of that duty.
neighbors.shared: peace is something people protect, not just hope for.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427 (Salok, Guru Tegh Bahadur) (paraphrase) · Guru Gobind Singh, Zafarnama, verse 22 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: five villages for peace
neighbors.text: The Mahabharata tells of a war that began with a peace mission. Before the great battle, Krishna himself went to the Kaurava court to plead for peace; tradition says the Pandavas would have settled for five villages. He was refused. Then, on the battlefield, the Bhagavad Gita opens with Arjuna setting down his bow, unable to fight his own family.
neighbors.difference: Christians hope for swords beaten into plowshares and differ on whether believers may fight. In the Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna, a warrior, to do his duty in a righteous war without hatred; Hindus read it both literally and as the battle within.
neighbors.shared: every war is worth one more try at peace first.
neighbors.sources: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Krishna's peace mission) (paraphrase) · Bhagavad Gita 1.47; 2.31 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: patience, the highest practice
neighbors.text: The Buddha prized today's word. The Dhammapada calls patience, long-suffering, the highest austerity. Centuries later, the teacher Shantideva wrote that no austerity equals patience, and that someone who angers you can even become your teacher, giving you the chance to practice it. Patience, khanti, is one of the perfections on the Buddhist path.
neighbors.difference: In the Bible, patience is love that waits, and longsuffering is part of God's own name. In Buddhist teaching, patience is a trained strength of mind that cools anger, modeled on the Buddha, not on a creator.
neighbors.shared: waiting with love is its own kind of strength.

neighbors.heading: patience and longanimity
neighbors.text: Catholics count today's virtue twice. Their Bible, from the Latin, lists twelve fruits of the Spirit: "charity, joy, peace, patience, benignity, goodness, longanimity, mildness, faith, modesty, continency, chastity." Aquinas told the two apart: patience bears what hurts; longanimity keeps waiting for a good that's slow to come. And bearing wrongs patiently is one of the works of mercy.
neighbors.difference: The King James, following the Greek, lists nine fruits and says longsuffering. Catholic teaching, following the Latin tradition, counts twelve, so patience and longanimity stand side by side.
neighbors.shared: some good things only arrive for those who can wait.
neighbors.sources: Galatians 5:22–23 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1832, 2447 (paraphrase) · Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 136, a. 5 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the wounded healer
neighbors.text: Psychology has a picture for today's river. Carl Jung wrote that only the wounded physician heals, an old picture often traced to the Greek myth of Chiron, a healer whose own wound never closed. Support groups run on a similar idea: someone who has walked through grief or addiction sits with someone just starting, and the comfort passes on.
neighbors.difference: Paul's comfort starts with God, the Father of mercies, and flows on through people. Jung's healer heals out of understanding his own wound; no God has to be named, though Jung himself took religion seriously.
neighbors.shared: what helped you through can help someone else through.
neighbors.sources: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections (paraphrase) · the Greek myth of Chiron

neighbors.heading: among the mourners
neighbors.text: Jewish tradition builds today's comfort into a week. During shiva, after a death, friends come to the mourners' home, often bringing food, and sit with them. The Talmud teaches visitors to wait for the mourner to speak first. And as they leave, they say: may the Omnipresent comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem.
neighbors.difference: Paul's comfort flows from God through Christ to his churches. The Jewish blessing names God HaMakom, the Place, and sets each mourner among a whole people who have grieved and been comforted before.
neighbors.shared: nobody should have to grieve alone at their kitchen table.
neighbors.sources: Talmud, Moed Katan 28b (paraphrase) · the traditional blessing for mourners (HaMakom yenachem)

neighbors.heading: from joy we came
neighbors.text: Today a catechism said we're made to glorify God and enjoy him forever. An Upanishad reaches for joy too. Bhrigu searches for Brahman, the ultimate, and at last sees it: from bliss, ananda, all beings are born; by bliss they live; into bliss they return. Hindu teaching names four aims of life, and the last is moksha, freedom.
neighbors.difference: The catechism's joy is a person enjoying a personal God forever. The Upanishad speaks of Brahman as bliss itself; some Hindu schools see the self at last as one with it, while devotional schools keep lover and Beloved.
neighbors.shared: joy isn't a side dish; it may be what we're for.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.6 (paraphrase) · the four aims of life (purusharthas) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: only that they might worship
neighbors.text: The Qur'an asks today's question too, and answers in one line: "I created the jinn and humankind only that they might worship Me." Muslim teachers read worship, ibadah, wide: prayer and fasting, and also honest work and kindness done for God. And the Qur'an promises that in remembering God, hearts find rest.
neighbors.difference: The catechism joins glory and joy with one and, and Christians give that glory through Christ. Islam names worship as the purpose, and rest of heart as one of its gifts.
neighbors.shared: knowing what you're for can steady a hard day.
